Question:
The perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) has already been explained; now the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) should be discussed. Answer:
The physical characteristics of valor and vigor, as well as valorous and vigorous activities, constitute diligence (*vīrya*).

Among these, when bodhisattvas—from the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) until the site of ultimate enlightenment—establish all wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind associated with the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), this is called the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).

Furthermore, if one practices diligence that is not shared with ordinary beings, nor with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—whether they be those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—this is called the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).
There are three kinds of diligence: namely, of body, speech, and mind.
That physical and verbal diligence is preceded by mental diligence; briefly stated, there are three kinds of meritorious activities.
If the body is engaged in a meritorious activity, this is physical diligence.
If it is associated with speech, it is verbal diligence (*vākkusīda*).
If it is associated with the mind, it is mental diligence (*manokusīda*).
Furthermore, when one engages in physical activity for the sake of either one's own benefit or the benefit of others within what is wholesome, this is physical diligence (*kāyakusīda*).
Vigorous conduct of speech is diligence of speech; vigorous conduct of mind is diligence of mind.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two kinds of bodhisattva diligence: namely, the diligence of not severing the lineage of the Three Jewels;
the diligence of maturing immeasurable sentient beings;
The diligence of embracing immeasurable cycles of transmigration;
the diligence of providing immeasurable offerings and service;
and the diligence of accumulating immeasurable roots of goodness.
The diligence of generating immeasurable vigor;
the diligence of skillfully teaching so as to gladden sentient beings;
and the diligence of establishing all sentient beings in peace and security.
The diligence of acting in accordance with the deeds of all sentient beings;
the diligence of practicing equanimity among all sentient beings;
and the diligence of undertaking the training in the precepts.
The diligence of being tamed and softened by the power of patience;
the diligence that gives birth to all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis;
and the diligence that fulfills unattached wisdom.
The diligence of accomplishing the four brahma-vihāras;
the diligence of giving birth to the five supernormal powers;
and the diligence of perfecting one’s own buddha-field with the merits of all buddha-fields.
The diligence of subduing all māras;
the diligence of subduing all non-Buddhist teachers in accordance with the Dharma;
and the diligence of fulfilling the Buddha-dharmas such as the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.
The diligence of adorning body, speech, and mind;
the diligence of accomplishing all that is to be done;
and the diligence of destroying all afflictions.

The diligence of causing those who have not crossed over to cross over, those who have not been liberated to be liberated, those who have not found rest to find rest, and those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa;
the diligence of accumulating the provisions for the marks of a hundred merits;
and the diligence of embracing all the Buddha-dharmas.
The diligence of wandering through boundless Buddha-fields;
the diligence of beholding immeasurable Buddhas.

These various forms of diligence arise from great compassion; they are free from body, speech, and mind; they abide in neither grasping nor rejecting; they attain neither elevation nor depression; and they encompass the non-arising and non-origination [of phenomena].
When these thirty-two factors are thus fully perfected, the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) shall be attained in its pure fulfillment.
Regarding this, there is also a sacred verse:
"Those perfections such as giving and the rest Are accomplished through the power of vigor."
Therefore, diligence is the root by which all bodhisattvas attain the Buddha-body.

Through the skillful means of diligence, they seek awakening; I consider diligence to be the supreme skillful means, for once one has abandoned diligence, skillful means cannot accomplish what is to be done.
If there were only a single means, then there would be no application of effort in performing tasks;
all that is accomplished is done through diligence. Therefore, diligence is the supreme means.
The mind possesses skillful power as its means; this mind arises from diligence.
Therefore, whatever tasks are undertaken, all have diligence as their foundation.
Through all treatises and arts and crafts, one reaches the further shore by means of diligence;
therefore, among all things to be accomplished, diligence is the most effective means of success.
All forms of mastery and wealth can be attained by those who possess diligence;
therefore, all matters of peace and happiness have diligence as their cause for attainment.
Because he possesses such preeminent diligence, the Buddha is the foremost among the śrāvakas;
therefore, this power of diligence is the most excellent cause, and no other practice is so.

Those who are supremely diligent and courageous, though remaining on the same stage among the various stages, always attain the most supreme excellence; therefore, one should constantly arouse diligence.
When the Buddha was beneath the Bodhi tree, he awakened to bodhi through diligence;
therefore, diligence is the root. The cause for attaining the Buddha-body has already been explained previously.
Question:
The perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) has already been briefly explained; now the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) should be discussed. Answer:

Regarding dhyāna, there are four kinds of dhyāna: namely, with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and possessing the joy and bliss born of seclusion, one dwells in the first dhyāna;
without directed thought and without sustained thought, and possessing the joy and bliss born of concentration, one dwells in the second dhyāna;
with the fading away of joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing bliss with the body, one dwells in the third dhyāna.
Having extinguished pleasure and pain, and with equanimity and mindfulness purified, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant.

Among these four types of dhyānas, when one has distanced oneself from realizing the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and has dedicated [the merit] toward the stage of a Buddha, it is called the dhyānapāramitā.

Bodhisattvas possess sixteen kinds of dhyānapāramitā that are not possessed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. What are these sixteen? They are: the dhyāna of non-appropriation of reality; the dhyāna of non-attachment to flavor; the dhyāna with great compassion as its object;

the dhyāna of the turning of samādhi; the dhyāna of manifesting supernatural powers; the dhyāna of mental mastery; the dhyāna of all samāpattis; the dhyāna of tranquility and further tranquility; the unshakable dhyāna; the dhyāna free from adverse conditions; the dhyāna of entering into wisdom; the dhyāna that accords with the mental activities of sentient beings; the dhyāna that ensures the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed; the dhyāna of non-retrogression; the dhyāna of mastery over all phenomena; and the dhyāna of dispersal.
These sixteen kinds constitute the dhyānapāramitā.
One does not grasp at actual dhyāna in order to fulfill the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
One does not cling to the flavor of dhyāna because one does not crave personal pleasure.
The dhyāna of the great compassionate object-condition is so called because it manifests the skillful means for severing the afflictions of all sentient beings.
The dhyāna of the turning of samādhi is so called because it takes the desire realm as its object-condition.
The dhyāna of manifesting supernormal powers is for the purpose of knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings.
The dhyāna of mental flexibility is for the purpose of accomplishing mastery over the mind through wisdom.
The dhyāna of various *samāpattis* excels all [dhyānas] of the form and formless realms.
The dhyāna of "tranquility and further tranquility" excels the *samāpattis* of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The dhyāna of immovability is so called because it reaches the ultimate limit.
The dhyāna of detachment from adverse conditions is so called because it eliminates the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The dhyāna of entry into wisdom is so called because it transcends all worldly realms.
The dhyāna that accords with the mental activities of sentient beings is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
The dhyāna that ensures the lineage of the Three Jewels is not severed is because the Tathāgata-dhyāna is inexhaustible.
The dhyāna of non-retrogression is because one constantly enters meditative absorption.

Regarding the dhyāna of mastery over all phenomena (*sarvadharmavaśitādhyāna*): because all karmas are fulfilled, the sixteenth [stage], the dhyāna of dispersal (*vidhvamsana*), is fundamentally missing and thus not explained.

Furthermore, there are: purity of mindfulness, purity of wisdom, purity of inclination, purity of shame, purity of maintaining the mind’s aspiration, purity of dedication to bodhi, purity of the faculties, purity of non-reliance, purity of non-apprehension of reality, and the arising of supernatural power.
The purity of thorough clarity; the purity of mental flexibility; the purity of physical seclusion; the purity of internal tranquility;
the purity of non-engagement externally; the purity of the view of non-apprehension; the purity of the absence of sentient beings, life-force, and person;
the purity of non-abiding within the three realms; the purity of the gateway of the factors of enlightenment; the purity of radiant light free from cataracts; and the purity of entry into wisdom.
Purity through non-contradiction of cause and effect; purity through the patient acceptance of reflecting on karma; purity through the wisdom that discerns the signs of the embryonic stages;

purity through the skillful means of gathering [beings] through prior ingenuity; purity through the removal of obstacles at the site of enlightenment; purity through non-attachment to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
purity through abiding in dhyāna and generating light; and the non-distraction of the Buddha-samādhi.
Purity, purity of observing the activities of one's own mind, and purity of knowing the various faculties of all sentient beings and teaching the Dharma accordingly—

these constitute the [first] three purities (the original text lacks two purities). Those sixteen kinds of dhyānapāramitā become pure by virtue of these thirty-two purities, thereby enabling entry into the stage of the Tathāgata.
In this regard, there is a verse:
"If those sixteen kinds, as well as the thirty-two purities,
are conjoined with the perfection of dhyāna, this constitutes the seeking of bodhi."
Having reached the further shore of dhyāna and skillfully understanding the workings of dhyāna, the wise one possesses the five supernormal powers and gives rise to them without falling back.
All forms are inexhaustible; he thoroughly penetrates their true nature.
With the supreme divine eye, they see all forms and appearances everywhere;
with the pure divine ear, they hear all sounds from afar.
Yet the wise, having attained thorough penetration, know that sound is not something that can be expressed in speech.
Regarding the minds of all sentient beings, observing their respective characteristics,
one sees that all minds are like illusions and understands their intrinsic nature.
One is able to recollect and know, exactly as they truly are, where sentient beings dwelt in their past lives.
All phenomena have no past, and one knows their intrinsic nature.
Going to the land of Universal Knowledge, one sees that land is fully adorned;
the characteristics of the land are like empty space, and one thoroughly understands its true nature.
The afflictions of sentient beings all arise from a distracted mind;
therefore, those of supreme wisdom extensively cultivate various meditative concentrations.
Question:
The brief explanation of the *dhyānapāramitā* is now complete; next, the *prajñāpāramitā* should be explained in sequence. Answer:
As previously explained, the *prajñāpāramitā* was taught within the context of the initial provisions (*sambhāra*).
I shall now further explain its characteristics.
As stated in the preceding verse:
"Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration—these are the five kinds [of perfections], and what remains [is wisdom]."
Those various pāramitās are subsumed within the pāramitā of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Beyond these, there are four other pāramitās, namely: the pāramitā of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna), the pāramitā of power (bala), and the pāramitā of knowledge (jñāna).
These four pāramitās are all subsumed within the prajñāpāramitā. As for the prajñāpāramitā:
when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sat beneath the Bodhi tree and awakened to all dharmas through the wisdom of a single moment of correspondence, that was the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, it has the characteristic of non-obstruction because it is bodiless;
the characteristic of boundlessness because it is equal to space;
and the characteristic of being unequaled because all dharmas are unattainable.
The characteristic of being far removed, because it is ultimately empty.
The characteristic of being invincible, because nothing can be apprehended.
The characteristic of being without phrases, because there is no body of names.
It has no characteristic of aggregation, because it is free from coming and going.
It has no characteristic of causality, because it is free from an agent.
It has no characteristic of arising, because there is no such thing as arising.
It has no characteristic of going or arriving, because it is free from cyclic flow.
It has no characteristic of disintegration, because it is free from the limits of the past and future.
It has no characteristic of defilement, because it cannot be grasped.
It has no characteristic of conceptual proliferation, because it is free from all conceptual proliferation.
It has no characteristic of movement, because it is the very essence of the dharma-realm.
It has no characteristic of arising, because it is non-discriminative.
It has the characteristic of being immeasurable, because it is free from measurement.
It has the characteristic of being without support, because there is no support.
It has the characteristic of being unstained, because it does not arise.
It has the characteristic of being unfathomable because it is without limit;
it has the characteristic of spontaneity because it knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the characteristic of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) as well as that which enters through correct reflection (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
The characteristics of that wisdom arising from hearing consist of eighty kinds, namely, aspiration and so forth.
There are thirty-two kinds of correct contemplative entry, namely, abiding in śamatha and so forth.
Furthermore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is not associated with the sixteen kinds of ignorance regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and so forth.
Thus, these characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā* have been explained according to their measure; were they to be explained in full, they would be immeasurable.

Within this perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalya-pāramitā) encompassed by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there are eight kinds of skillfulness: namely, skillfulness regarding the aggregates (skandha-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding the sense-bases (āyatana-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding the truths (satya-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding the three times (tryadhva-kauśalya), skillfulness regarding the various vehicles (yāna-kauśalya), and skillfulness regarding all phenomena (dharma-kauśalya).
In this regard, skill in the perfections (*pāramitā*) is without limit.

Furthermore, according to whichever realm of rebirth and by whatever mode of conduct, for the sake of awakening, one attains the further growth of one's own roots of virtue and the taming of sentient beings.

Regarding those various modes of rebirth and those various courses of action, whatever diverse skillful means ought to be practiced in all such instances have been analyzed and taught by the Great Beings; I shall now speak of but a tiny drop from among those sūtras.
If one has already performed or is currently performing even a slight good deed, being able to cause it to become much or immeasurable—this is skillful means.
Acting not for oneself but solely for the sake of sentient beings—this is skillful means.
Using *dāna* alone to bring all the *pāramitās* to fulfillment is the skillful means (*upāya*).
Likewise, using *śīla* to encompass all places of birth; using *kṣānti* to adorn body, speech, and mind for the sake of *bodhi*;
using *vīrya* to abide in diligence; and using *dhyāna* so as not to regress from meditative concentration.
Through *prajñā*, one abandons the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one acts as a refuge and protector; through compassion (*karuṇā*), one does not forsake saṃsāra;

through sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one is able to endure that which is unpleasant; through equanimity (*upekṣā*), one initiates all virtues; through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one encompasses the Buddha-eye;
through the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), one fulfills the Buddha-ear; and through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), one knows [the thoughts of others].

With their respective faculties, they know the three periods of time through the recollection of past lives without obstruction; through sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they attain the sovereign supernormal powers of a Tathāgata;

by entering the minds and desires of sentient beings, they know the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); having already crossed over, they re-enter [the world]; being unstained, they appear stained;
having laid down the burden, they take up the burden again; they manifest the immeasurable as measurable, and the most supreme as inferior.
By means of skillful means, they are associated with nirvāṇa yet remain within the cycle of saṃsāra; though they practice nirvāṇa, they do not abide in ultimate quiescence.
They manifest the four māras yet transcend all māras; they realize the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths and contemplate non-arising, yet do not enter the fixed stage of the śrāvaka.
Though they move amidst the clamor of the world, they do not engage in the underlying tendencies of affliction.
Although they practice seclusion, they do not rely on the exhaustion of body and mind; although they traverse the three realms, they do not practice worldly conventions within those realms;
although they practice emptiness, they constantly seek the Buddha-dharma at all times;

although they practice the unconditioned, they do not realize the unconditioned as a final attainment; although they practice the six supernormal powers, they do not exhaust their outflows. Although...
While manifesting the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not abandon their aspiration for the Buddha-dharma.

One should know that all such skillful means within the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) for teaching and transforming sentient beings constitute the dwelling place of a bodhisattva’s skillful means of transformation.
In this regard, there is a verse:

The various sufferings and afflictions within the realm of animals, And likewise those born as hell-beings or hungry ghosts— These are experienced in accordance with the cycle of transmigration; Such are the manifold faults and evils of sentient beings.
This mass of suffering cannot obstruct them; they give rise to compassion toward sentient beings.
Thus the Buddhas declare those bodhisattvas to possess unimpeded compassion for all the world.
If there is anything in the treatises that is well-comprehensive, whether it be the works produced by various individuals,
the sciences of crafts and so forth, or other matters, he bestows them all upon others with loving speech.
The wealth of precepts, learning, cultivation, tranquility, and self-mastery—by means of these merits one gathers and transforms others;
having gathered them, one causes them to continue perpetually. The Supreme Sage has declared this to be dwelling in the path of goodness.
Sometimes manifesting in a female body to transform men, causing them to be tamed and receive instruction;
sometimes manifesting in a male body to transform women, causing them to be tamed and receive instruction.
If they do not weary of the pleasures of defiled objects, out of compassion for those lacking the Way to lead them into it,
they transform beings through various gateways according to their dispositions, never abandoning them even in the most extreme states of suffering.
Some may have faith and understanding in non-self, and know that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature;
yet such persons have not yet transcended worldly dharmas, but merely engage in such contemplation.
Though one has faith and compliance toward karma and its results, there are boundless matters of suffering;
when it comes time to undergo those bitter fruits, one will not rejoice as one is oppressed by various sufferings.
If there are those who have gone forth as śrāvakas, he places them in a state of peace and tranquility, or again in the path of the pratyekabuddhas;
or he places them in the vehicle of the ten kinds of wondrous powers, so that they may attain the vehicle of perfect enlightenment; or they may attain tranquility and rebirth in the celestial realms.
If one should observe the visible fruits and correctly apply them as they were performed,
then from the beginning until the ultimate end, a man of resolve can accomplish even difficult tasks;
by relying on those various skillful means, he abandons all that is pleasant and unpleasant.
This vehicle is praised by all Buddhas, adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits;
it can produce the utmost pure faith in the world, for it expounds the supreme and wondrous path of goodness.
Within the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, as well as among all the vehicles of the devas and the world,
they bring beings to maturity through the ten wholesome paths of action, and likewise mature human beings within the human vehicle.
Having already explained the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), I shall now speak of the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
From the very beginning, bodhisattvas have ten great aspirations; namely, to provide offerings and attend to all Buddhas without exception—this is the first great aspiration.
To uphold the Great True Dharma maintained by those Buddhas, to embrace the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and to universally protect the True Teaching—this is the second great vow.

Whenever Buddhas appear in all worlds, from their initial residence in the Tuṣita Heaven through their descent and entry into the womb, their dwelling in the womb, their birth, their renunciation, their realization of Perfect Awakening, their being requested to turn the Wheel of Dharma, until their entry into Great Nirvāṇa—to go to each of those places to receive, practice, and make offerings to them without ever abandoning them—this is the third great vow.

The fourth great vow is: to give rise to and produce such minds as these—minds that encompass the vast and immeasurable practices of all bodhisattvas; that are subsumed by the various *pāramitās* and are pure through being unmixed with other paths; that bring forth the general and specific classifications, the common and distinct characteristics, and the shared and unshared modes of all bodhisattva practices; that are taught according to reality and the true path; and that consist of the cultivation of the *pāramitās*, the instructions, and the exhortations, which, once bestowed, are maintained and sustained. This is the fourth great vow.

There is no realm of sentient beings—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—who dwells within the three realms and the six destinies together, encompassed by the process of birth and the succession of name-and-form, who has not all been brought to maturity, led into the Buddha-dharma, had their various destinies severed, and established in the knowledge of all modes; this is the fifth great vow.

There are other worlds without exception—vast and immeasurable, whether subtle or coarse, horizontal or inverted, or abiding level—that enter together and dwell in common; they proceed toward the ten directions in every part like a net of Indra, entering into each division and proceeding in accordance with wisdom. This is the sixth great vow.

All lands are one land, and one land is all lands; these infinitely pure and equal lands are universally adorned, free from all afflictions and fully endowed with pure requisites, filled with sentient beings possessing immeasurable marks of wisdom. Entering the supreme and wondrous realm of the Buddhas, they manifest according to the minds of sentient beings to bring them joy—this is the seventh great vow.

To share the same mind as all bodhisattvas; to gather roots of goodness that are not shared with others; to share the same objects of focus as all bodhisattvas and never be separated from the equality of bodhisattvas; to initiate one’s own mind so as to enter the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; to attain the supernormal powers of non-retrogressive practice; to travel through all worlds; to reach all great assemblies like a shadow and engage in discourse; to accord with and enter all places of birth by means of one's own body; and to be fully endowed with the inconceivable Mahāyāna—this is the eighth great vow.

In order to ascend to the practice of non-retrogression and perform the bodhisattva deeds; in order that the actions of body, speech, and mind may not be in vain; in order that at the very moment of seeing [the Buddha], one may become certain of the Buddha-dharma; in order that at the very moment of uttering a single sound, one may enter into wisdom; in order that at the very moment of faith, one may transform the afflictions; in order to obtain a body like that of the Great Medicine King; and in order to practice all the bodhisattva deeds—this is the ninth great vow.
It is for the sake of perfectly awakening to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within all worlds;

it is for the sake of manifesting birth, sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering great *parinirvāṇa* within a single pore-path as well as within all other pore-paths;
and it is for the sake of entering the great realm of the Buddha through wisdom.

By virtue of his majestic spiritual power, he manifests for the sake of all realms of sentient beings, awakening them according to their profound inclinations at the time when a Buddha should appear, so that they may attain tranquility;
because he has perfectly realized that all phenomena are of the single nature of nirvāṇa;
because he utters a single sound to cause the hearts of all sentient beings to rejoice; and because he manifests...
Because of the power of uninterrupted practice within Great Nirvāṇa; because of manifesting the ground of great wisdom to establish all dharmas;
and because of pervading all worlds with the dharma-knowledge and supernormal powers of the Buddha-realm—this is the tenth great vow.
Such are the great desires and great productions, of which the ten great vows are the foremost.

Having fulfilled these ten great vows, one establishes hundreds of thousands of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) further vows of a bodhisattva and attains the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); this is called the perfection of vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
The perfection of aspiration has already been explained; I shall now speak of the perfection of power.

In this context, it is briefly stated that bodhisattvas possess seven kinds of powers: namely, the power born of karmic maturation, the power of supernormal knowledges, the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of samādhi, and the power of prajñā.
Regarding the power born of karmic reward: the strength of ten small elephants equals the strength of one dragon-elephant;
the strength of ten dragon-elephants equals the strength of one fragrant elephant; the strength of ten fragrant elephants equals the strength of one great fragrant elephant;
the strength of ten great fragrant elephants equals the strength of one great athlete; and the strength of ten great athletes equals that of half a nārāyaṇa.
Regarding the power of extension: ten and a half Nārāyaṇa powers equal one Nārāyaṇa power; ten Nārāyaṇa powers equal one Great Nārāyaṇa power;
ten Great Nārāyaṇa powers equal the power of a bodhisattva who has passed one hundred kalpas;
and ten powers of a bodhisattva who has passed one hundred thousand kalpas equal the power of a bodhisattva who has passed one hundred thousand kalpas.
The power of a bodhisattva over a hundred thousand kalpas is equal to the power of one bodhisattva who has attained patience (kṣānti);
the power of ten such bodhisattvas who have attained patience is equal to the power of one bodhisattva in their final birth (caramabhavika).
Having established himself in this power, the Bodhisattva was able to take seven steps immediately upon birth.
The strength of a Bodhisattva in his final birth is equal to the strength of a Bodhisattva in his youth.
Having established himself in this power, the bodhisattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment and attains equal and perfect awakening.

Having attained perfect awakening, by virtue of a power of merit exceeding hundreds of thousands, he accomplishes the Tathāgata’s single power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-jñānabala).
The accomplishment of these ten powers is called the power born of the karmic retribution of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and a small portion of other sentient beings.

As for the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), it refers to having well-cultivated and frequently practiced the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); by means of this rare power of supernormal faculties, one is able to discipline and transform all sentient beings.
By means of his rare and wondrous supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he manifests forms, powers, or modes of sustenance (*dhāraṇa*).

If there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by a particular form or appearance, he manifests that very form or appearance to those respective beings—whether as the form of a Buddha, the form of a Pratyekabuddha, or the form of a Śrāvaka; likewise, the form of Śakra, Brahmā, a World-Protector (*lokapāla*), or a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*); or again, any other form, even down to the form of an animal.
For the sake of taming sentient beings, he manifests such forms and appearances.

If there are sentient beings who are powerful, arrogant, wrathful, cruel, and self-exalting, and who can be tamed by means of power, he then manifests such power—whether it be the strength of a great athlete, or the strength of a quarter-Nārāyaṇa, or half a Nārāyaṇa, or the full strength of a Nārāyaṇa.

By this power, he takes up Sumeru, the King of Mountains—sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas high and eighty-four thousand yojanas wide—with three fingers as easily as picking up an *āmalaka* fruit, and hurls it to another world-system; yet the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three suffer no affliction, nor does the Bodhisattva’s strength diminish.
Furthermore, although this trichiliocosm is vast and expansive, from the water element up to the Peak of Existence, he could place it upon the palm of his hand and remain there for an eon.
He fully manifests such powers through his mastery of the various supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).

If there are sentient beings who are arrogant, conceited, wrathful, violent, or self-exalting, he teaches the Dharma to subdue them, causing them to abandon arrogance, conceit, anger, violence, and the like.

Having attained such knowledge of sustaining through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he was able to sustain whatever he desired by means of that sustaining knowledge: if he were to turn the great ocean into a cow’s footprint, it would become a cow’s footprint; if he were to turn a cow’s footprint into the great ocean, it would become the great ocean; if he were to turn the conflagration at the end of an eon into a mass of water, it would become a mass of water; if he were to turn a mass of water into a mass of fire, it would become a mass of fire; if he were to turn a mass of fire into a mass of wind, it would become a mass of wind; and if he were to turn a mass of wind into a mass of fire, it would become a mass of fire.

Thus, if one sustains [the teachings] in this manner, then once the inferior, middling, and superior dharmas have been sustained according to their respective levels, no one will be able to shake them or cause them to vanish.

That is to say, whether it be Śakra, Brahmā, Māra, or any other worldly beings who share similar dharmas—with the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—among all classes of sentient beings, there is no being capable of shaking, disturbing, or causing the disappearance of the dharmas sustained by the Bodhisattva, because of the power of that sustaining.
For the sake of those sentient beings who possess various forms of supreme joy, exultation, and reverence, he preaches the Dharma.

With the power of his supernormal feats (ṛddhi) rising high and acting with mastery, he transcends the afflictions of Māra, enters the realm of the Buddhas, awakens all sentient beings, and gathers the provisions of roots of goodness from past lives; neither Māra nor the gods of Māra’s host can obstruct him.
This is called the bodhisattva’s power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
As for the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*), it is the resolute conviction within the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as within the bodhisattva practices, which cannot be thwarted or destroyed.

If an evil Māra should come in the form of a Buddha, seeking to destroy the bodhisattva’s faith in any given teaching, the bodhisattva—by virtue of the power of their resolute belief—will remain unmoved by that Māra’s attempts to undermine their strength of faith.
This is called the power of faith.
As for the power of diligence: when a bodhisattva arouses diligence and accords with various wholesome dharmas, he attains firm strength in those respective instances.
Whatever practice one undertakes, whether as a deva or a human, it cannot be shaken or destroyed, nor can one be made to cease within it;
this is called the power of diligence (*vīryabala*).
As for the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), when one dwells in various states of phenomena, the mind remains settled and composed, such that no other afflictions can cause distraction.

By means of upholding [the mind] through the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*), one destroys all afflictions (*kleśa*); those afflictions cannot destroy what the bodhisattva is mindful of. This is called the power of mindfulness. As for the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*):

while in the midst of bustle and clamor, one practices the conduct of seclusion. Various sounds and whatever issues from the path of speech do not act as thorns or obstacles to the first dhyāna; practicing wholesome applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) does not obstruct the second dhyāna; the arising of affectionate joy (*prīti*) does not obstruct the third dhyāna; and maturing sentient beings, gathering all dharmas, and never abandoning or neglecting them does not obstruct the fourth dhyāna.
Thus, by practicing these four kinds of dhyāna, he cannot be destroyed by any adverse conditions opposing the dhyānas.
Although he practices these dhyānas, he is not reborn according to them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s power of samādhi.

The power of *prajñā* refers to indestructible wisdom regarding both mundane and supramundane phenomena; throughout successive births, without relying on the instruction of a teacher, the Bodhisattva brings before him all activities, fields of craftsmanship and sciences, and even those things most difficult to perform or endure that are supreme in the world.
If supramundane dharmas rescue the world, once the bodhisattva’s wisdom has entered in accordance with them, the hosts of devas, humans, and asuras cannot destroy it.
This is called the power of prajñā.
Thus have the seven powers of the bodhisattvas been briefly explained; were one to expound them in full detail, they would be without limit.
This is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of power (bala-pāramitā).
Having already explained the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), I shall now explain the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

Herein, there are the worldly practices such as writing, treatises, seals, calculation, and arithmetic; the science of elements (*dhātu-śāstra*) concerning the natures of wind, bile, phlegm, and mucus; and the science of regions (*deśa-śāstra*), namely medical treatises that cure diseases such as consumption, insanity, and possession by spirits, as well as neutralizing various poisons. Furthermore, there are compositions consisting of jokes and humorous banter intended to produce joy.

They manifest birth in villages, cities, gardens, groves, ponds, lakes, wells, and springs; they display the natures of precious substances such as gold, silver, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, and conch-stones white as mother-of-pearl or jade, as well as coral and other gems; they enter into matters such as solar and lunar eclipses, the movements of the stars, earthquakes, and strange dreams; and they establish the various marks on the body, including the limbs, joints, and members.

One knows the perfections of the spheres of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, supernormal powers, the immeasurables, and the formless realms, as well as other perfections corresponding to perfect awakening that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Furthermore, he knows the formation and destruction of all worlds; he fully understands how worlds form according to their formation and how they are destroyed according to their destruction.
Moreover, he knows that worlds are formed because of the accumulation of karma and are destroyed because karma is exhausted.
He knows for how long the world remains in the state of formation and maintenance; he knows for how long the world remains in the state of destruction.
He knows the distinctions among the earth element, water element, wind element, and fire element, whether they be great, small, or immeasurable.
He knows the most subtle atoms, as well as the aggregation and dispersion of all atoms.
He knows the number of earth-atom particles within all worlds, and likewise he knows the number of water, fire, and wind-atom particles.
They know the number of body-atoms of all sentient beings and the number of body-atoms of their lands.

They know the distinctions between the coarse bodies and subtle bodies of all sentient beings, and they even know how the bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, devas, and humans are composed of the aggregation of atoms.
They know the formation and destruction of the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as their distinctions of small, large, and immeasurable.

They know the karmic bodies, retribution bodies, and physical bodies within the bodies of sentient beings; they know the small, large, defiled, and pure states within the bodies of lands, as well as the distinctions of the networks of directions, such as horizontal, inverted, and level abidings.
He knows the bodies distinguished by various names within the body of karmic retribution;
he knows the bodies distinguished by various names within the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;

and he knows within the body of a Tathāgata the body of perfect enlightenment, the body of vows, the transformation body, the sustaining body, the body adorned with physical forms and marks of excellence, the body of majestic radiance, the body of mental intention, the body of merit, and the dharma-body.

Within the body of wisdom, one knows: whether it be skillful discernment, or reflection in accordance with reality, or inclusion within the correspondence of results; whether mundane or supramundane; whether established as the three vehicles; whether common or uncommon dharmas; whether the path of emergence or not the path of emergence; and whether [the state of] training or beyond training.

Knowing that within the Dharmakāya there is equality and immobility, one establishes the locations and names of conventional truth, establishes the dharmas of sentient beings and non-sentient beings, and establishes the Buddha-dharma and the noble Saṃgha.
One knows the immeasurable bodies within the body of space, entering the distinctions of the true, boundless, and formless bodies that are non-bodies in all places.
One attains the wisdom of producing such bodies as these.

Furthermore, they attain mastery over life, mastery over the mind, mastery over requisites, mastery over karma, mastery over vows, mastery over resolute belief, mastery over supernatural powers, mastery over wisdom, mastery over birth, and mastery over the Dharma.
Having attained these ten masteries, one becomes a possessor of inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, and non-retrogressive wisdom.
Such wisdom comprises eighty-four thousand modes of activity; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
Thus has the perfection of wisdom been explained according to its divisions; were one to wish to expound it in its entirety, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would be able to elucidate it.
These six perfections are the total provisions for enlightenment, just as within the expanse of space all things are fully contained.

As explained regarding the six pāramitās, they encompass all the provisions for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra); just as all things moving and stationary within space—whether sentient or insentient—are entirely contained therein.

In this way, it should be understood that the remaining accumulations, such as the accumulation of hearing and so forth, are subsumed within the six perfections; they share the same characteristics and are no different.
