Furthermore, there is the opinion of other masters that all the provisions for enlightenment...
"True relinquishment and tranquil wisdom are subsumed under four bases.
Furthermore, another master of the treatises reflects:
"All the provisions for enlightenment are subsumed under the base of truth, the base of relinquishment, the base of tranquility, and the base of wisdom."
Reality is the characteristic of being non-deceptive; reality itself is ethical discipline (*śīla*), and therefore reality constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Renunciation is giving (*dāna*); therefore, the sphere of renunciation constitutes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Quiescence is the mind being unperturbed; if the mind is unperturbed, it cannot be moved by objects of affection or aversion. Therefore, the state of quiescence constitutes both the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
The station of wisdom is, in turn, the perfection of prajñā.
The perfection of vīrya enters into all stations; for without diligence, nothing can be accomplished in any station. Therefore, the perfection of vīrya brings all matters to fulfillment.
Therefore, all provisions enter into these four bases.
Question:

As the Sūtra says, one attains an unimpeded mind through the provision of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and one attains the severance of hatred and affection through the provision of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In this regard, what is the distinction between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)? Answer:
Great compassion penetrates to the very marrow of the bones; it serves as the refuge for all sentient beings.
Just as a father’s love for his only son extends universally to all, so too does compassion pervade everything.

Even if one enters the perilous paths of saṃsāra, falls into the various realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, remains caught in the net of evil and false views, is shrouded by the dense forest of ignorance, or wanders upon deviant paths and non-ways like one in blind darkness—mistaking what is not liberation for liberation, seized by the bandits of old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair, and entering the thicket of Māra’s intent—[compassion remains].

Those who are far removed from the Buddha’s intention [should know that] the great compassion of a bodhisattva pierces through their own skin, flesh, and sinews down to the marrow of the bones, acting as a refuge for all sentient beings. This causes these beings to cross over such a wilderness of birth and death, its perilous and evil paths, and establishes them in the fearless palace of the city of omniscience.

It is like an elder who has an only son of great merit who falls ill; his love penetrates through the skin and flesh to the very marrow of the bones, and he thinks only of when that son’s illness might be cured.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is likewise: it arises only toward suffering sentient beings, whereas loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arises toward all sentient beings without exception.
Furthermore, through loving-kindness, one attains an unimpeded mind toward all sentient beings; through compassion, one never grows weary or exhausted amidst the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, loving-kindness arises toward those who are virtuous, while compassion arises toward those who are unvirtuous.

Moreover, because the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness increases, they do not cling to their own happiness and thus give rise to great loving-kindness; because their compassion increases, they relinquish their limbs, members, and even their lives, and thus give rise to great compassion.
If one recollects the Buddha’s merits and hears of the Buddha’s miraculous transformations,
receiving them with love and joy, this is called "great joy.
Regarding the recollection of the Buddha’s merits, what therein constitutes the Buddha’s merits?
This refers to the fact that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have accumulated roots of goodness throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas;

because they do not guard [the need for concealment] regarding their actions of body, speech, and mind; because they have severed doubt within the five things to be known; because they are without fault in the four ways of answering difficult questions;
because they provide instruction on the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; and because of the twelvefold dependent origination.
Because of awakening as a pratyekabuddha within birth; because of teaching the nine teachings; because of being fully endowed with the four modes of sustaining the Dharma;
because of attaining the four immeasurables; because of fulfilling the six pāramitās; because of expounding the ten stages of the bodhisattva;
because of the perfection of the five supramundane aggregates; and [because of] the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Because he is fully endowed [with all qualities], because his sphere of activity is boundless, because he exercises sovereign mastery over his own mind,
because he possesses a nature that is never satiated, because he has attained the vajra-like samādhi, because his preaching of the Dharma is never in vain,
because his teachings cannot be subverted, because he is the guide of the world, because no one can see the crown of his head, and because there is none equal to him.
Because it is invincible; because it is an inconceivable dharma; because it attains great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
because of the marks of a hundred merits; because of immeasurable roots of goodness;
because of boundless merit; because of immeasurable merit; because of innumerable merit; because of merit that is beyond conceptual differentiation.
Because of their rare and marvelous qualities, and because of their unique, unshared qualities—these and others are called the various qualities of the Buddhas upon which one should reflect.

In order to transform all sentient beings, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest supernatural transformations through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). According to the beings who are to be delivered, according to their bodies, according to the dimensions of their forms—whether long or short, broad or narrow—and according to the various distinctions of their species and their pure, differentiated voices, the Buddhas employ various rare supernormal powers; in accordance with their conduct and their inclinations and desires, they teach and transform them through those respective diverse skillful means and miraculous manifestations.
Having heard this, the experience of joy, delight, and purity is called "great joy" (muditā).

Within the mind, mental vigor is called "love" (prīti); when this love pervades the body, it is called "joy" (muditā); the awakening of pleasure within the joyful mind is called "feeling" (vedanā); and at the time of experiencing that pleasant feeling, recollecting the virtues of the Great Supernatural Powers of the Perfectly Enlightened One so that the mind remains unturbid is called "purity" (śuddhi).
When that mind is pure, it is filled with joy; this is called "great joy" (*mahāmuditā*).
Although those who have ascended the limited vehicles (*hīnayāna*) also possess joy, it is designated as "great joy" because it is not shared [with them].
Question:
Should a bodhisattva abandon sentient beings, or should they not abandon them? Answer:

A bodhisattva should not abandon sentient beings; rather, according to their capacity, they should sustain them at all times. A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly keeps in mind the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

If they are afflicted by greed, hatred, and delusion, or if they have ascended onto the path of stinginess, breaking precepts, resentment, indolence, distracted minds, and evil wisdom, or have entered onto divergent paths—such beings should not be abandoned. At all times, one should teach them generosity, ethical discipline, and meditation, and according to what is within one's power, one should sustain them and never cast them aside.
From the very beginning, a bodhisattva should, according to their capacity and strength, employ skillful means to transform sentient beings and cause them to enter the Mahāyāna.

This refers to the bodhisattva who has ascended to the Mahāyāna; among sentient beings, they should act from the outset according to what they are capable of, employing the very same skillful means as those explained previously in the *Pāramitā* section on skillful means. They should diligently apply various skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, establishing them in this Mahāyāna.
Question:
For what reason do bodhisattvas teach and transform sentient beings solely through the Mahāyāna, and not through the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas? Answer:
If one were to transform sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to attain the fruit of Arhatship;
yet if one were to transform even a single person and lead them into the Mahāyāna, this merit would be superior.

Even if one were to teach and transform sentient beings equal in number to the sands of the Ganges so that they attained the fruit of Arhatship, the merit of this Mahāyāna would surpass the merit of teaching and transforming those of the Śrāvaka and other vehicles, because its seeds are inexhaustible.
All these seeds can serve as the skillful means for other sentient beings to generate the bodhicitta;
furthermore, because they also give rise to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, this merit is superior to that [other merit].
This merit is superior because the Mahāyāna is supreme compared to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
furthermore, the bodhicitta possesses immeasurable and incalculable merit.
Furthermore, because the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed through the Mahāyāna,
those who seek great merit should instruct and transform sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna, and not by other vehicles.
Question:
Do the Mahāsattvas teach and transform sentient beings solely by means of the Mahāyāna, and not by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna?
Answer:
Regarding those taught by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna and the Pratyekabuddha-yāna:
because they possess little strength, they are incapable of being transformed by the Mahāyāna.

If there are sentient beings of middling or inferior disposition who abandon the task of benefiting others and lack great compassion, and are thus incapable of being transformed by the Mahāyāna, one then transforms and delivers them by means of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Question:
If there are sentient beings who cannot be transformed by means of the three vehicles, should one abandon them or not?
Answer:
Those who are incapable of being transformed through the vehicles of the śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, or even the Mahāyāna, should be established in the realm of merit.

If there are sentient beings who delight in birth and death and loathe liberation, and who cannot be transformed by the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna, they should be taught and established within the Brahma-vehicle of the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra).

Furthermore, if there are those who cannot be transformed by the Brahma-vehicle, they should be taught and established in the heavenly vehicle, in the ten paths of wholesome action, and in meritorious deeds such as giving; they must not be abandoned.
Question:
If there are sentient beings who delight in worldly pleasures and lack the power to practice the three types of meritorious deeds, what should one do for such persons?
Answer:
If there are those who cannot endure [the teachings on] heaven and liberation, one should instead gather them through worldly benefits according to their capacity.

If there are sentient beings who single-mindedly seek sensual pleasures and do not contemplate the next world, tending toward the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—such that they cannot be taught to be born in heaven or attain liberation—one should likewise pity them as being like children in wisdom. One should gather them through worldly means as appropriate, employing giving and other virtues according to one's own power, pitying them and never abandoning them.
Question:

If a bodhisattva finds that there is no skillful means by which they can convert or guide sentient beings who possess these characteristics of being like small children, what should they do toward such persons?
Answer: Toward sentient beings, a bodhisattva possesses the capacity to teach and transform them without [ordinary] conditions;
they should give rise to great compassion and must not simply abandon them.

If a bodhisattva encounters sentient beings who delight in evil and are pitiable, yet lacks the skillful means to guide and transform them, that bodhisattva should regard them as his own children and arouse great compassion; there is no reason whatsoever to abandon them.
Question:
It has already been stated that one must embrace sentient beings; however, the method for such embracing is not yet known. Answer:
Giving and gathering through teaching the Dharma, Furthermore, listening to the teaching of the Dharma,
And also practicing deeds that benefit others— These are the skillful means of gathering.
In order to gather and sustain sentient beings, the various Bodhisattvas may employ giving as a skillful means of gathering, or they may accept what is given by others.
Sometimes they preach the Dharma for others, or listen to others preaching the Dharma;
sometimes they practice altruism through beneficial speech (*priyavāditā*) or through collaborative conduct (*samānārthatā*);

sometimes they explain the various fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), or instruct in the arts and crafts (*śilpa-kalā*), or demonstrate manual labor; sometimes they cause the sick to recover, or rescue those in perilous distress.
These and others like them are called the skillful means for gathering in sentient beings.
One should gather in sentient beings by means of these various skillful means; one should not abandon them.
Question:
Having gathered in sentient beings through such skillful means of gathering, what benefit is accomplished?
Answer: Whatever benefit one performs for sentient beings, it is done without weariness and without negligence.
To give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment is to benefit oneself by benefiting the world.
Herein, when a bodhisattva makes a vow to benefit the world, they generate this intention:
"Whatever serves to benefit the world, I shall perform it all."
Having made this vow, one should not grow weary or negligent in performing deeds for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"To benefit the world is itself to benefit oneself."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abandon the causes and conditions for bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Question:

It has already been stated that a bodhisattva should constantly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings and should not practice renunciation; however, among all phenomena, should they be renounced or not?
Answer: Entering the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one extinguishes and departs from conceptual discrimination;
being entirely without effortful application, one spontaneously relinquishes all sense bases.
The dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); therefore, it was previously stated:
whether a Tathāgata appears or does not appear, this dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), remains eternally constant—namely, dependent origination.
Furthermore, as previously stated:
"Ānanda! Dependent origination is profound, and its realization is also profound."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva enters this profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they extinguish all extremes of existence and non-existence; having grasped the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), they immediately sever all stirring thoughts, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and discrimination. They become detached from all signs of grasping, and the spheres of activity of mind, intellect, and consciousness no longer function. Even the practices of the Buddhas, the practices of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*), the practices of bodhisattvas, and the state of nirvāṇa are no longer practiced. Thus, they are without further effort regarding all phenomena, attaining within all phenomena a mind of stillness and further stillness, a non-conceptual mind. This is called the relinquishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-upekṣā*).
This is precisely the non-conceptualization of the bodhisattva.
Having already explained supramundane equanimity, I shall now explain mundane equanimity:
Regarding gain, fame, praise, and pleasure— One remains unattached in these four spheres.
Conversely, there is also no obstruction; these are called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

Being unattached to gain, fame, praise, pleasure, and the like, and conversely, not being hindered or discouraged by the absence of gain, lack of fame, blame, or suffering, one abandons both love and hatred and dwells in the middle without further discrimination. This is called the second explanation of worldly equanimity.
Question:

If a bodhisattva practices the relinquishment of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-tyāga*) regarding all phenomena, how can such diligent practice as that of one who would burn their head and clothing for the sake of awakening be possible?
Answer: For the sake of enlightenment, until the point of non-retrogression,
a bodhisattva should practice with such diligence as one whose head or clothing is on fire.

Although one should thus relinquish all phenomena, a bodhisattva must resolutely practice as if their head or clothing were on fire; until they attain the stage of non-retrogression, a bodhisattva should diligently strive for the sake of enlightenment.
Among these, one should know that there are five kinds of causes and conditions for a bodhisattva’s non-retrogression from awakening. What are the five?

As stated in sūtras such as the *Kusuma-avataṃsaka*, they are: hearing the names of bodhisattvas who possess great vows and of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and aspiring to be born in the lands of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. These constitute two kinds of causes and conditions.
Because of upholding and expounding profound sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the third causal condition.
Because of cultivating and attaining through sympathetic joy the samādhis such as "abiding in the presence," this is the fourth causal condition.
These four causes and conditions explain the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

However, if this bodhisattva, having already entered the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, they are said to be ultimately and definitively non-retrogressive.
Question:

If a bodhisattva can attain non-retrogression through any one of these four causes and conditions, how does that which was previously stated—that they should practice with diligence as if their head or clothing were on fire—become fulfilled?
Answer: Indeed, when those bodhisattvas seek awakening,
they must not cease their diligence, for they bear a heavy burden.
Although a bodhisattva attains non-retrogression through any one of the four causal conditions, they must not cease their diligence, because they have previously made this vow:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa."
Because they bear such a heavy burden, they apply themselves with diligence without ceasing during that interval.
Question:
For what reason do they not find rest in their diligence during that interval?
Answer: Until the patience of great compassion has arisen, even though a bodhisattva has attained non-retrogression,
they may still die because they give rise to negligence.

Among the four causal conditions, whichever condition a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva may encounter, if they have not yet given rise to great compassion and have not yet attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they will undergo death and rebirth through the power of karma during that interval due to falling into negligence.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice with diligence as if their head or clothing were on fire, in order to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), remaining tireless in their vigor throughout that interval.
Question:
What further deaths does a bodhisattva undergo?
Answer: If one enters the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is as death;
for it severs all the faculties of understanding and knowledge belonging to a bodhisattva.
Regarding the four kinds of causes and conditions previously mentioned, by whichever of these one may attain non-retrogression:

this bodhisattva has not yet attained great compassion, nor has he attained patience (*kṣānti*); he has not yet transcended the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Due to the influence of evil friends, out of fear of the suffering of birth and death, or because of taking birth in the intermediate state, or during the period of the destruction of an eon when he feels resentment toward bodhisattvas and slanders the true Dharma, he loses the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Having given rise to the mind of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha stage, he may then realize the liberation of a śrāvaka or the liberation of a pratyekabuddha. By doing so, he severs the root of a bodhisattva—namely, great compassion.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas and Buddha-Bhagavāns are said to be those who understand death through explanation and realization.
Question:
This should be considered: does a bodhisattva fear dwelling in the hells, or does he fear falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha?
Answer: Even if they were to fall into the hells, Bodhisattvas feel no fear;
yet the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are for them a source of great terror.

Even if a bodhisattva were to dwell in the hells, enduring countless hundreds of thousands of sufferings, this would not be comparable to the fear of falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Question: Why is this so?
Answer: Falling into the hells does not ultimately obstruct bodhi;
rather, the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha constitute ultimate obstructions.
Even if one enters hell, it cannot constitute an ultimate obstacle to the path of perfect enlightenment.
While dwelling in hell, it serves as a temporary obstacle to the path of bodhi only until the limit of that evil karma has been exhausted.

If a bodhisattva falls into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, they will never again arise; therefore, the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha constitute obstacles to the path of perfect enlightenment.
For this reason, a bodhisattva’s entry into the hells is not comparable to the fear of falling into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Question:
What is that fear like?
Answer: As it is said: "Just as one who cherishes life fears decapitation, so should one fear the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
In the sūtras, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has spoken thus:
"Just as one who cherishes life fears decapitation,
so too should a bodhisattva who seeks unsurpassed awakening fear the stages of the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha."
Therefore, although a bodhisattva may enter the hells, this is not comparable to the fear of falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Question:
You have already explained the obstructive factors for bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
How does this bodhisattva attain the patience of non-arising? Answer:
It is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is not the case that it is neither arising nor ceasing.
It is not taught as being both together nor as being neither; the same applies to emptiness and non-emptiness.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination, they form this thought:

"The phenomena that arise dependently are merely conventional designations, like the existence of arising within non-arising. Therefore, the intrinsic nature of arising is not established; because its intrinsic nature is not established, arising does not exist."
Just as arising itself does not exist, its cessation constitutes a duality, and both are without intrinsic nature.
Just as with arising and cessation, non-arising and non-cessation constitute a duality, and these two likewise both lack intrinsic nature.
Within those two types—arising and ceasing—neither non-arising nor non-ceasing exists, because they are mutually contradictory.
Emptiness is also like this.
Just as that which exists has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so it is with that which is not empty, and with that which is both empty and not empty.
Question:
If one holds the view that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they arise dependently, why then does one further hold the view that there are no dependently arisen phenomena either?
Answer: Whichever phenomena may exist, to observe them therein without wavering is the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, for it severs all conceptual discrimination.
When a bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination in this way according to reality, they attain freedom from the view of an intrinsic nature in all phenomena.
Because they are free from the view of an intrinsic nature, they immediately sever the grasping for the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
When one attains the realization of the self-nature of dharmas, one forms this thought:
"It is not that internal and external dharmas do not exist, yet there is no self-nature of dharmas.
Although there are dependently arisen dharmas, they are like a bundle of reeds, a magical illusion, or a dream."
If a phenomenon arises from conditions, its own intrinsic nature does not arise.
Having contemplated in this way, one cannot be shaken by any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, yet one does not realize [nirvana] prematurely.
Because he contemplates the non-arising of phenomena with joy and severs all conceptual discriminations, it is called "patience regarding non-arising.
This bodhisattva then dwells in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi).
The verse says:
Having attained this patience, one immediately receives the prophecy:
"You shall certainly become a Buddha."
They immediately attain non-retrogression.

Because they have attained this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), at the very moment of attainment—neither before nor after—all Buddhas appear before them and bestow the prophecy of their future buddhahood, saying:
"In a future age, at such a time, in a certain world and during a certain eon, you shall become a certain Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
This is called the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva.
Question:

Since all bodhisattvas from those dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage are definitely directed toward triple enlightenment (*triyāna-sambodhi*), why are they not said to be "non-retrogressive," while only bodhisattvas dwelling in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) are so designated?
Answer: Those bodhisattvas who abide in immovability have attained the non-retrogressive wisdom of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Since that wisdom cannot be overturned by those of the two vehicles, they alone receive the name "non-retrogressive."

This refers to all supramundane roots of goodness, such as faith and so forth, which cannot be obstructed or caused to regress by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even bodhisattvas dwelling in the seventh bhūmi; therefore, they are called "non-regressive.
It does not mean that the other ten types of bodhisattvas are non-regressive regarding all dharmas for the sake of full enlightenment (sambodhi).
The causes and conditions for non-retrogression have already been explained; herein, one further receives a superior prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

In the Mahāyāna, four kinds of predictions are taught: the prediction for those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta, the prediction for those who have resolved upon bodhicitta together with others, the concealed prediction, and the manifest prediction. These constitute the four kinds of predictions.

Regarding those among them who have not yet generated the bodhicitta but receive a prediction of enlightenment: these individuals possess sharp faculties and are endowed with superior faith; having observed them with their unimpeded Buddha-eye, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, grant them this prediction.

Regarding the bestowal of prophecy upon those who have together resolved to attain bodhicitta: having matured their roots of goodness and planted the seeds of bodhi, they have previously practiced so that their faculties have become sharp and they have attained superior progress. Because they desire solely to liberate all sentient beings, at the very moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they enter the stage of non-retrogression; they possess no quality of falling back and are free from the eight unfavorable conditions, namely the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).
If this person were to hear their own prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), they might fail to exert diligence in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā);
however, if they do not hear it, they will instead arouse even greater diligence.

To ensure that [the person] does not hear it—desiring to cause others to hear their prediction so that their doubts may be severed—the Buddha employs his majestic spiritual power (prabhāva) to conceal the prediction.

If a bodhisattva brings the five supramundane faculties to maturity, attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and dwells in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they receive a prophecy of enlightenment in their very presence.
These are the four kinds of prophecy.

Because those bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) are already established in certainty, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) upon them in their presence.
Furthermore, there is another prophecy based on intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), which serves as the fifth, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"We all rejoice in the intentional words of the Great Sage."
Just as the noble Śāriputra was fearlessly prophesied,
so shall we also attain Buddhahood, the Unsurpassed One in the world;
furthermore, through words of intentional meaning, he spoke of our supreme perfect enlightenment.
For what reason is this distinct expression of prophecy spoken?
A certain master of the treatises says:
it is for the purpose of causing those śrāvakas who have not yet entered the state of certainty to resolve upon bodhicitta.

Furthermore, for those beginner bodhisattvas who have already resolved upon awakening but fear the suffering of saṃsāra and wish to attain parinirvāṇa in the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas, [this is taught] in order to make their resolve for awakening firm.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas from other buddha-fields gathered here for whom the time for their prediction has arrived; they are given predictions under names that correspond [to those of their respective fields].
While the various masters thus distinguish these different modes of prophetic declaration, as for the actual meaning therein, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to know it.
Until the Bodhisattva attains the samādhi in which all Buddhas dwell manifest before him, he should not give rise to negligence.
"Dwelling after having attained the samādhi in which all Buddhas are manifest before one" refers to the samādhi in which the Buddhas of the present appear and abide before his very presence.
Samādhi means abiding in equanimity.
Until a bodhisattva has attained this samādhi, they must not be negligent in the interim.
Because as long as samādhi has not been attained, the bodhisattva may still fall into the evil destinies and has not yet escaped from the states of non-leisure.
Therefore, in order to attain this samādhi, one should not be negligent;
if one attains samādhi, one will be liberated from all those fears.
This samādhi is of three kinds: namely, that which has form as its object, that which has dharmas as its object, and that which is without an object.

Among these, if one recollects the Buddha by taking as an object the Tathāgata’s body adorned with the primary and secondary marks, this is the samādhi of objective support for form (*rūpa-ālambana-samādhi*).

Furthermore, if one recollects the Buddha by taking as an object the immeasurable categories of the Buddha’s qualities—such as the ten titles, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-dharmas—this is the samādhi of objective support for phenomena (*dharma-ālambana-samādhi*).

Furthermore, if one does not take form as an object of focus, nor takes dharmas as an object of focus, and likewise does not bring the Buddha to mind through mental attention, and there is nothing to be attained—this samādhi of emptiness, which is far removed from all signs, is called the "samādhi without objective support."

Among these, a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening attains the samādhi that takes form as its object; one who has already entered the practice takes dharmas as their object; and one who has attained the patience of non-arising is without any object.
These are called "attaining certainty" because of their mastery.
The Buddhas dwell manifest before them; this firm samādhi is the father of the bodhisattvas, and great compassion and patience are their mother.

Because these three aforementioned samādhis—the Buddhas of the Present Abiding Before One—encompass all the merits of bodhisattvas and all the merits of Buddhas, they are called the fathers of all bodhisattvas.

One who possesses great compassion is called a "mother" because they do not give rise to weariness amidst the流转 (saṃsāra) of birth and death, and because they protect others from falling into the perilous precipices of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding "patience": a bodhisattva who has attained patience does not weary of the cycle of existence amidst the sufferings of saṃsāra, nor does he abandon sentient beings or bodhi.
Because they do not give rise to revulsion, this patience is also the mother of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, another verse says:
"Prajñāpāramitā is the mother; Upāya is the father."
Because it gives birth to them and sustains them, it is called the mother and father of bodhisattvas.
Since the *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, the Buddha has said that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of the bodhisattvas.

Once the dharmas of all bodhisattvas have arisen from the perfection of wisdom, they are sustained by skillful means so as not to cause them to fall into the perilous precipices of the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Because they maintain awakening through this, skillful means are said to be the father of bodhisattvas.
Question:
By how much merit can a bodhisattva attain awakening?
Answer: By accumulating even a small amount of merit, one cannot attain bodhi;
only by gathering merit equal in measure to a hundred Sumerus can one attain the supreme state.
Bodhi refers to the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
That knowledge should be understood as equal to non-existence (*abhāva*), and that which is to be known (*jñeya*) should be understood as equal to space (*ākāśa*).

Because space is limitless, that which is to be known is also limitless; for one cannot attain limitless knowledge through merit that has limits. Therefore, by accumulating even a small amount of merit, one cannot attain bodhi.
How is it attained?
It can be attained only when a mass of merit equal in measure to a hundred Sumeru mountains has been accumulated.
*Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
*Bodhisattvapiṭaka-bhāṣya* (Treatise on the Provisions for Enlightenment), Volume Four.
Original by the Noble Nāgārjuna; explained by the Bhikṣu Īśvara;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of South India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
Question:
If this is so, since there would be no accumulation of merit even equal in measure to a hundred Sumerus, not a single person would be able to attain bodhi.
Answer:
Even when performing small meritorious deeds, there is a skillful means here:
one should give rise to a mental focus toward all sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva performs even a small merit with such skillful means, they will thereby bring about a great accumulation of merit.

Whether by giving food and drink to sentient beings, or by offering flowers, incense, garlands, and so forth to images of the Tathāgata, they take all such merit and direct it as an object of focus toward all sentient beings encompassed within all worlds, thinking:
"By this merit, may all sentient beings attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
furthermore, may I share this merit with all sentient beings."
Dedicating such merit, together with all sentient beings,
toward Bodhi is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva.
By dedicating in this manner, that merit becomes immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless.
For this reason, although that knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is indeed boundless, it can nevertheless be attained by means of these very marks of boundless merit.
Furthermore, there is another meaning.
Whatever actions I perform, I always do for the benefit of sentient beings.
Who could measure the merit of such mental activities?
During both day and night, the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to such mental activities.

Whatever wholesome actions I perform through body, speech, and mind, they all arise for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, liberating all sentient beings, providing relief to all sentient beings, and bringing all sentient beings to nirvāṇa; and they are for the sake of causing sentient beings to fulfill the knowledge of all modes and to attain the knowledge of all modes.
Thus, for one who is fully endowed with great compassion and dwells securely in skillful means, who—except for the Buddhas—could possibly measure the mass of their merit?
Therefore, one who possesses this merit is able to attain bodhi.
Question:
Why is this merit, moreover, immeasurable?
Answer: One does not cherish one's own kin, nor body, life, or wealth;
one does not crave the pleasures of sovereignty, nor the Brahma world or other celestial realms.
Nor do they crave for nirvāṇa; for the sake of sentient beings, they think only of sentient beings—how can anyone measure their merit?

In this regard, when a bodhisattva practices the six perfections, for the sake of sentient beings, they have no attachment whatsoever to their own children or grandchildren, nor to their relatives; whether it be wealth such as gold and silver, their own life, their limbs and members, their entire body, physical or mental pleasure, sovereignty over gods and humans, the Brahma-heaven realm, the formless heavens, or even nirvāṇa—they do not cherish any of these. They think only of sentient beings with compassion and do not abandon them.

"What shall I do so that these sentient beings—children, ordinary folk, and the ignorant who are blinded by the cataracts of ignorance—may be liberated from the prison of the triple world and established in the city of nirvana, which is eternal, blissful, and fearless?"
Thus, when a bodhisattva practices deeds for the benefit and happiness of others, loving all sentient beings without cause, who could possibly measure their merit?
Furthermore, a verse says:
For those in the world who have no refuge or protector, He provides protection from their suffering and distress.
Who could measure the merit of one who gives rise to such thoughts and practices?
This Bodhisattva constantly brings forth great compassion and reflects thus:

"In this world, there is no savior and no protector; beings wander throughout the six realms of existence, entering the fires of the three sufferings. Having no refuge, they run hither and thither, their bodies and minds perpetually afflicted by various ailments and distress."
To those who have no refuge or protector, I shall provide a place of reliance and rescue them from all the sufferings experienced by their bodies and minds.
Who could possibly measure the merit of generating such thoughts and actions?
If one practices in accordance with the Perfection of Wisdom for even as long as it takes to milk a cow,
or for one month, or many months, who could measure its merit?
This Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and brings to fulfillment the dharmas of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If a bodhisattva were to contemplate and cultivate that mass of merit for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, it would still be immeasurable;

how much more so if they practice in conjunction with it for one day and night, two days and nights, three days and nights, up to seven days and nights, half a month, one month, or even many months—by whom could such a mass of merit be measured?
The profound sūtras praised by the Buddha, Which one recites oneself, teaches others,
And explains in detail for them— This is called a mass of merit.
"Profound" refers to the profound sūtras.
That which accords with emptiness and transcends the world is profound;
furthermore, it is because it is analyzed as dependent origination.
Dependent origination is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the body of the Tathāgata.
Those who possess a body in correspondence with that of the Tathāgata are those for whom this profound sūtra has been praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Whether reciting it themselves, teaching others to recite it, or explaining it to others, they do so without a mind of expectation, desiring only that the body of the Tathāgata not be allowed to perish.
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, for the purpose of causing it to abide for a long time.
Who could possibly measure the merit belonging to that [act],
which causes immeasurable sentient beings to resolve their minds toward Bodhi?
The treasury of merit increases further and becomes most excellent; one shall attain the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Herein lies a bodhisattva skilled in means who first gathers all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); knowing that those beings have accepted his words, he then instructs them to resolve upon *bodhicitta*.
When a bodhisattva who is thus endowed with skillful means causes sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta, the merit they thereby generate cannot be measured by anyone, for it is immeasurable.
Furthermore, because it causes all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta, the treasury of merit becomes even more exalted.
It is called a "treasury of merit" because merit is inexhaustible; since it can reach the state of inexhaustibility, it cannot be exhausted.
Regarding the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*): it is called the Immovable Ground because it cannot be shaken.
Herein, because the Bodhisattva causes others to generate the bodhicitta, his own bodhicitta remains unshaken and undiminished throughout successive lifetimes;
and because he causes others to generate the bodhicitta, this very act becomes the cause for the Immovable Ground.
Following and turning the supreme wheel of Dharma turned by the Buddha—
which pacifies all thorns of evil— is the merit-treasury of the Bodhisattva.

Just as the World-Honored Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in the Abode of Seers near Vārāṇasī, so too is it a treasury of merit to turn that most excellent wheel of Dharma in accordance with it.

There are three causes and conditions for this conforming transformation: namely, regarding the profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata which accord with emptiness and transcend the world, whether one upholds them, explains them, or practices in accordance with the Dharma.
If one maintains such sūtras as these so that they are not lost, this is the first way of turning the wheel of Dharma in accordance with it.
To analyze and expound them for sentient beings who possess the capacity [for understanding], this is the second way of turning the wheel of Dharma in accordance with it.
As stated in that sutra, practicing in accordance with the Dharma constitutes the third turning of the wheel of Dharma in conformity.

Regarding "extinguishing all thorns of evil": the thorns of evil in the Buddha's teaching refer to the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as well as Māra—the sovereign of the desire realm—who hates liberation.

If there should be anyone among the fourfold assembly who speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or speaks what is not the Teacher’s instruction as the Teacher’s instruction—these are evil thorns within the Buddha's teaching. You should subdue them in accordance with the Dharma, crushing their pride and destroying their wrong views so that the Dharma may flourish.
This is called the pacification of all thorns of evil;
because it pacifies these thorns of evil, it is named the Bodhisattva’s treasury of merit.
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, they endure the great sufferings of hell.
How much more so for other minor sufferings, when awakening rests in the palm of one's hand!

If a bodhisattva dons the firm armor and constantly generates a mind of diligent effort for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, then for the sake of liberating even a single being, they would remain within the great Avīci hell for kalpas, enduring hardship with unwavering fortitude; how much more so for other minor sufferings.
If a bodhisattva can endure such sufferings as these, one should know that awakening (bodhi) rests in the palm of their right hand.
Their actions are not for their own sake, but solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings;
because all this arises from great compassion, awakening resides in the right hand.

Whatever actions a bodhisattva undertakes, such as giving and so forth, are performed solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings and to enable them to attain nirvāṇa, due to the power of great compassion; they never act for the sake of even the slightest personal pleasure, and thus they too are truly great compassionate ones.
Know that for such a great person, bodhi has come to their right hand.
Wisdom is free from conceptual proliferation; diligence is free from indolence;
renunciation is free from stinginess—bodhi rests in the right hand.
Question:
Since the various pāramitās, such as dāna and the others, have already been explained previously, what is the purpose of explaining them again now? Answer:

Previously, I explained this for the sake of practitioners; now, I explain it for those who possess the light of the wisdom of non-apprehension and patience, because they perceive the characteristic of the single path. Through that wisdom, they are far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
through not relinquishing their yoke, their diligence is far removed from indolence;
and through the elimination of craving, their generosity is far removed from stinginess.
Thus, one should know that for such a bodhisattva, awakening has come to their right hand.
With concentration free from dependence and discursive thought, with the perfection of untainted precepts,
and with the patience of the non-arising of phenomena— awakening rests in the right hand.

If a bodhisattva has successfully accomplished the dhyāna-pāramitā, this concentration does not rely upon the three realms; its characteristic is tranquility, free from discursive thought and perception.
Furthermore, they fulfill ethical discipline (śīla) that is unadulterated and untainted, dedicating it toward enlightenment without any decay.

Furthermore, having successfully accomplished the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one abides in the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) within the context of dependently originated phenomena; because this root is supreme, there is no regression.
One should know that awakening (bodhi) then rests in the palm of one's right hand.
Question:
It has already been explained how bodhisattvas who have practiced and attained patience accumulate various fields of merit, and how this accumulation of merit can lead to awakening.
How does a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on awakening accumulate various fields of merit, such that this accumulation of merit can lead to awakening?
Answer: To all the Perfectly Awakened Ones currently dwelling throughout the ten directions,
I stand before each of them and confess my unwholesome deeds.

If there are present Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who dwell throughout the worlds of the ten directions without obstruction, remaining there for the sake of benefiting sentient beings through the power of their original vows.
Now, before these realized ones, I confess all my transgressions:

whatever evil karma I have committed myself, incited others to commit, or rejoiced in the commission of, throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra—whether in past lives or in the present—arising from greed, hatred, and delusion through body, speech, and mind, I declare them all and dare not conceal them; I shall sever them forever and never commit them again.
In those worlds of the ten directions, wherever a Buddha has attained enlightenment but does not yet proclaim the Dharma,
I pray that he turn the wheel of the Dharma. If the World-Honored Buddha,

having fulfilled his great vows and realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, should remain with few desires and dwell in tranquility, refraining from turning the wheel of the Dharma for the sake of the world— [I pray that he will do so].

I shall exhort that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, to turn the wheel of the Buddha-dharma, for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of devas and humans.
To all the Truly Awakened Ones currently existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions, who now wish to relinquish their life-span: I prostrate and entreat you to remain.

If the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who are unimpeded in the world, have realized Bodhi in the ten directions, turned the wheel of Dharma, and established the True Dharma, and if the multitudes who were to be transformed have already been fully transformed, yet they now wish to relinquish their life-span—[I entreat them to remain].

I shall prostrate before that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and entreat him to remain for a long time, to benefit many people, to bring peace and happiness to many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the great assembly of devas and humans.
Whatever merit from generosity and precepts arises from the body,
speech, and mind of all sentient beings— whether through reflection or cultivation,
whether by noble ones or ordinary people, and throughout the worlds of the past, present, and future—

I rejoice in all accumulated merit. Whatever meritorious deeds performed by sentient beings—such as giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation—which arise from body, speech, and mind, whether already accumulated, currently being accumulated, or yet to be accumulated; and whatever merit belongs to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, buddhas, bodhisattvas, and other noble ones, as well as that of ordinary worldlings—in all these, I rejoice.

To rejoice in this manner is the foremost, the preeminent abider, the extraordinary, the supreme, the most excellently gathered, the exquisite, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled; to rejoice in this way is truly called rejoicing.

If all the merit I possess were gathered into a single lump and dedicated to all sentient beings so that they may attain perfect enlightenment; if all the accumulations of merit I have acquired since beginningless saṃsāra—

whether toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or individuals, down to the gift of a single morsel of food to an animal— as well as the roots of goodness from taking refuge, the roots of goodness from repentance, the roots of goodness from requesting [the turning of the wheel], and the roots of goodness from sympathetic joy— all these were weighed together and made into one lump.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I dedicate [these merits] toward enlightenment and relinquish them all.
By means of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings realize unsurpassed perfect awakening and attain the wisdom of all-knowledge.
I thus confess my transgressions, entreat [the Buddhas], rejoice in merit, and dedicate it toward enlightenment; know that this is just as the Buddhas do.

Whether it be the roots of goodness from dedicating them toward enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, the roots of goodness from confession, the roots of goodness from requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the roots of goodness from requesting long life, or the roots of goodness from rejoicing—all these are weighed together as a single lump. Just as the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, when they were bodhisattvas, have already dedicated or shall dedicate their roots of goodness, I likewise dedicate all these roots of goodness toward enlightenment.
By dedicating these roots of goodness, may I and all sentient beings realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
I shall now speak further in brief:
I confess my sinful evils and entreat the Buddhas to rejoice in my merit.
And as for the dedication toward enlightenment, it is as the Most Victorious One has taught.

One should confess all one's own transgressions, request the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, pray that he remain for a long time, rejoice in all merits, and dedicate those merits; just as in the previous dedication for the sake of enlightenment, one should dedicate in this manner, exactly as the Most Victorious One has taught.
Question:
Furthermore, how should that dedication be performed? Answer:
Placing the right knee upon the ground and adjusting the upper robe over one shoulder, one should perform this practice three times each day and night with palms joined.

One should personally purify oneself by wearing clean garments, washing the hands and feet, and ensuring the lower robe is properly arranged; having adjusted the upper robe so it covers one shoulder, one places the right knee on the ground. With palms joined and a single-minded focus free from discursive thought, one should direct the mind toward a stūpa of the Tathāgata, or an image, or toward the space before one, visualizing all the Buddhas as dwelling right there in person.
Having formed this intention, as previously described, one should perform it three times each during the day and three times at night.
If the merit produced in a single session were to have a physical form,
even a great trichiliocosm as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not be able to contain it.

Regarding the dedication performed during the six periods mentioned therein, if one were to distinguish the merit produced in even a single period, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones who see things as they truly are, have declared:

if that merit were to possess form like a heap of grain, its accumulation would be so immeasurable that even the entirety of three thousandfold world systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, could not contain it.

Because that merit is dedicated in a manner equal to the realm of empty space, even a single instance of such dedication possesses a mass of merit so vast; how much more so when there are many dedications?
Although this is a bodhisattva who has only newly resolved their mind, by the power of dedication they also achieve great merit.
Through such a mass of merit characterized in this way, they are able to gradually attain enlightenment.
Question:
It has already been explained how Bodhisattvas achieve the means for attaining great merit.
Now, wishing to protect that merit, by what means should one do so?
Answer: Once they have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment],
they should give rise to respect and love for all lesser bodhisattvas, just as they do toward their teachers, parents, or children.

If a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening wishes to protect their own roots of goodness and their own person, they should give rise to a heart of supreme respect and affection toward all bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon awakening, just as one feels toward the World-Honored One, the Teacher of All-Knowledge, or toward one’s own biological parents.
In this way, one should likewise cultivate the utmost affection and respect for all bodhisattvas, beginning with those who have first resolved their minds toward awakening.
If one acts otherwise, both oneself and one's roots of virtue will be utterly extinguished.
As the Blessed One once said in a sutra:
"I do not see any other single dharma that obstructs a bodhisattva or causes the extinction of their roots of goodness as much as the arising of a mind of malice toward a bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva, despite having accumulated roots of virtue over a hundred eons, should cause them all to perish by giving rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva,
one should therefore regard all bodhisattvas with respect, as if they were one's own teacher.
Even though a bodhisattva may have faults, they should still not speak of them;
how much less so when there is no basis in reality? One should only offer praise according to the truth.

If a bodhisattva reviles the faults of one who practices the Mahāyāna, causing that person to incur an ill reputation, all their wholesome dharmas throughout successive lives will be utterly extinguished, and they will be unable to increase their pure qualities (*śukladharma*).

Therefore, although bodhisattvas may have faults and evils, they should not speak of them openly for the sake of protecting the life of their own roots of goodness; how much less so when they are unreal, just like the crimes of a king.
As it is said in the sūtra:

There was a bodhisattva whose livelihood was pure and beyond reproach; yet because the bhikṣu Dharmaruci slandered him, he suffered the retribution of the hells for seventy kalpas, and for sixty thousand lifetimes he was a poor man, constantly afflicted by blindness, muteness, leprosy, and malignant sores.

Therefore, regarding a bodhisattva, one must not speak of either faults or their absence; rather, because they possess genuine virtues, one should only praise them. This is for the sake of increasing one’s own roots of goodness and also for the sake of inspiring faith in others.
If a person aspires to become a Buddha and wishes to remain non-retrogressive,
[the Buddha] manifests and blazes forth, causing them also to give rise to joy.
If there are sentient beings who have already made the vow to seek Bodhi, he desires only that they do not regress.
Yet there are those who, out of folly, hatred, and greed, and because they belong to their own faction, speak thus:
"What is the use of practicing the long and difficult bodhisattva conduct?"
The bliss of their nirvāṇa is equal and similar; by practicing the conduct of the śrāvakas, they swiftly attain nirvāṇa.
These matters will later be explained regarding their karmic fruition.
To manifest the Buddha’s merits through various analogies so that they enter the mind is what constitutes "manifestation."
To cause them to be fully endowed with the bodhisattva practices of diligence is "blazing";
to cause their diligence to increase further in speed and sharpness by explaining the matters of the great supernormal powers and the merits of perfect enlightenment is "joy."
In this way, cause them not to abandon the mind of enlightenment.
Do not say that profound sutras are not the Buddha's teaching;
if one speaks in such a manner, they will receive the most bitter and evil retribution.

The "profound sūtras" refer to those spoken by the Buddha that accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); which eliminate immeasurable extreme views such as nihilism and eternalism; which extinguish the inherent nature of the self, the person, sentient beings, and the life-span; and which reveal the Tathāgata’s great supernormal powers and rare virtues.
If you have not yet personally realized the truth contained within these sutras and vinayas, do not, out of ignorance, claim that they were not spoken by the Buddha. Why is this?
The World-Honored Buddha has taught that if one slanders the sutras spoken by the Tathāgata, the resulting evil fruit will be most bitter.
If all the various sins of the *ānantarya* class were gathered together into a single lump,
they could not equal even a fraction of the two previous types of sins.
Thus the World-Honored One said in the *Avaivartacakrasūtra*:
Regarding all the offenses of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*); or the karmic retribution for taking the lives of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm;
or the destruction or burning of *caityas* belonging to as many Buddha-Bhagavats as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River after they have entered parinirvāṇa;
or the obstruction of the Dharma of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

All such faults as the retribution for the eyes' transgressions are gathered together; yet when one develops attachment toward a profound sūtra that has not yet been understood and claims it was not spoken by the Buddha,
or causes a bodhisattva who has already made the vow for enlightenment to retreat from the mind of awakening—
these two kinds of offenses, compared to the aforementioned five ānantarya crimes and their like, [are far more grave].
A hundredth part does not equal it; a thousandth part does not equal it;
nor do even a numerical fraction, a *kara* fraction, a calculable fraction, a metaphorical fraction, or even a *upanisad* fraction equal it.
Because of these characteristics of sin, in order to protect oneself and one's own roots of goodness, one must not commit these two kinds of offenses.
Question:
It has already been stated that a bodhisattva protects their own roots of goodness.
What is the ultimate meaning of the path of cultivation? Answer:
One should skillfully practice the three gates of liberation.
First is emptiness, next is signlessness, and the third is wishlessness.
Within this context, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate these three gates of liberation.
First, one should cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness in order to disperse and dismantle all views.
Second is the gate of liberation of signlessness, in order not to grasp at the conceptual mind that clings to objects of perception.
The third is the door of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), for the purpose of transcending the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Question:
Why are these called "doors of liberation"?
Answer: Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; being already empty, how could they produce signs?
Since all signs are thus stilled, what could a wise person aspire to?
Because they arise dependently, phenomena lack intrinsic nature; this is called emptiness.
Because they are empty, the mind has no object of attachment, which is signlessness.
Being free from all signs, there is nothing for which one can form an aspiration.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon arises from conditions, its intrinsic nature is unarisen.
Because its intrinsic nature is unarisen, that phenomenon is empty.
If a phenomenon is empty, within it there is no characteristic.
Because marks do not exist, they are markless.
If there are no marks, the mind has nothing upon which to rely; because it has no reliance, the mind has no aspiration within the three realms.
When practicing mindfulness in this way, one approaches the path to Nirvāṇa;
do not dwell on what is not the essence of the Buddha, and do not be negligent regarding it.
When practicing these three gates of liberation, if they are embraced by skillful means, one approaches Nirvāṇa.
Although one should practice, do not fall into other states of awakening; one should seek the patience of non-apprehension and abide in skillful means.
Within nirvāṇa, I should not realize it immediately.
One should give rise to such a mind and bring the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to maturity. One should resolve:
"I shall benefit all sentient beings and deliver all sentient beings; although I cultivate the three gates of liberation, I shall not realize nirvāṇa."
Nevertheless, for the sake of studying the Prajñāpāramitā, I must exclusively bring the three gates of liberation to maturity.
I should cultivate emptiness, but I should not realize emptiness;
I should cultivate signlessness, but I should not realize signlessness.
I should cultivate wishlessness, yet I should not realize wishlessness.
Just as a master archer shoots arrows, each one piercing the next in succession,
holding them so they do not fall— so too it is with the Great Bodhisattva.
It is like a master archer who, having trained well in archery, shoots an arrow into the air and then continuously releases subsequent arrows, each striking the preceding one.
As those arrows become numerous, they support one another in mid-air, preventing them from falling to the ground.
Within the emptiness of the gates of liberation, he skillfully releases the arrow of the mind;
maintaining it with the continuity of skillful means, he does not allow it to fall into nirvāṇa.

Thus, this Bodhisattva, a great archer, having trained in and cultivated the bows of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, releases the mental arrow into the emptiness of the three gates of liberation. Furthermore, by means of the arrows of skillful means born of compassion for sentient beings, he successively maintains that mental arrow within the void of the triple world, preventing it from falling into the city of nirvāṇa.
Question:
How, furthermore, is that mind prevented from falling into nirvana? Answer:
I do not abandon sentient beings, for the sake of benefiting them.
First I give rise to such an intention, and thereafter I practice the corresponding application.
Once I have fully matured in the three gates of liberation, I would wish to take up nirvāṇa as if it were in the palm of my hand.

However, because these children are ordinary worldlings who are like those drinking milk, and because they are unable to head toward the city of Nirvana on their own and have not yet attained Nirvana, I should not enter Nirvana alone.
I shall thus arouse diligence; whatever I do, it shall be solely for the benefit of all sentient beings, and also so that all sentient beings may attain nirvana.
First, one should initiate the practice in this manner; next, the mind becomes compliantly associated with the three gates of liberation.
"Compliant" (anuloma) means conforming to what follows.

If it were not thus, because that arrow of the mind would lack the skillful means of integration, at the time of practicing the three gates of liberation, one would fall into the liberation of a śrāvaka or the liberation of a pratyekabuddha.
Now there is yet another skillful means:
those sentient beings who are attached, whether for a long night or in the present life,
their inversions and various marks all arise from the cause of delusion.

All childish ordinary beings, due to their delusion, have for a long night since beginningless time wandered in saṃsāra, clinging to the four inversions: they take the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be pleasure, the impure to be pure, and non-self to be self; furthermore, within the internal and external aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, they calculate "self" and "what belongs to self," claiming there is something to be attained, having practiced thus for a long night and practicing so even now.
For those who are attached to signs and inverted in their views, the Dharma is taught for the purpose of severing these attachments.
First, one should give rise to such a mind; subsequently, one practices in accordance with it.
Thus, because these sentient beings are deluded by ignorance, they give rise to the two kinds of clinging: the notion of "I" and the notion of "mine."
Furthermore, within the non-existence of form and so forth, they falsely give rise to conceptualization and grasp at signs, thereby producing four kinds of false inversions.
I have taught the Dharma for them so that they may eliminate these.
Having first generated such a mind, one subsequently cultivates the application of the three gates of liberation.
If one were to cultivate the three gates of liberation in any other way, one would instead be approaching the path to nirvāṇa.
That a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings yet perceives no sentient beings—
this too is the most difficult of matters, rare and inconceivable.
That a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of sentient beings— this too is most difficult, inconceivable, and unprecedented, like painting the sky.

In the ultimate sense, sentient beings have never existed from the very beginning; yet this bodhisattva, neither knowing nor perceiving them as such, exerts diligent effort for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings.
Except for Great Compassion, where else could there be such a difficult matter?
Although he has entered the stage of certainty and practices the gates of liberation,
because his original vow is not yet fulfilled, he does not realize nirvana.
This should be considered:

when a bodhisattva who has reached the stage of certainty enters that state of certainty by means of the thirty-two dharmas and becomes associated with the gates of liberation, in the interim before his original vow is fulfilled, does he realize nirvana or not?
For it is said in a sutra of the World-Honored One:

"The four great elements may be altered, but there is no bodhisattva who has entered the stage of correct determination (samyaktva-niyāma) who, in the interim before fulfilling their original vow, would realize nirvana."
Therefore, a bodhisattva who has reached the stage of certainty does not realize nirvāṇa until their original vow is fulfilled.
Even if they have not yet reached the stage of certainty, because they are sustained by the power of skillful means,
they likewise do not realize nirvāṇa as long as their original vow remains unfulfilled.

If a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment has not yet reached the stage of certainty, because they are sustained by skillful means, when they practice the three gates of liberation, they do not realize nirvana midway even before their original vow is fulfilled.
Extremely weary of saṃsāra, yet still moving toward it;
with faith and delight in nirvāṇa, yet turning away from it.

This bodhisattva, within the midst of saṃsāra, should feel extreme revulsion because of the three kinds of blazing fires, yet should not give rise to a mind that seeks to flee from saṃsāra; rather, they should move toward saṃsāra by regarding all sentient beings as their own children.
Furthermore, one should have faith and delight in *nirvāṇa*, as it is like a sheltered dwelling that provides protection.
Yet, one must also turn away from *nirvāṇa* in order to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If there is weariness with and detachment from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), then there will likewise be faith and delight in *nirvāṇa*.
If one neither flows toward saṃsāra nor turns away from nirvāṇa, yet has not yet fulfilled one's original vow while practicing the gateways to liberation, then one realizes nirvāṇa.
One should fear the afflictions (*kleśa*), but one should not exhaust the afflictions;
rather, one should gather a multitude of virtues to obstruct and suppress the afflictions.
Because this is the cause of saṃsāra, one should fear the afflictions (kleśa), yet one should not completely exhaust them.
If one were to sever the afflictions, one would be unable to accumulate the provisions for awakening (bodhisambhāra).

Therefore, the bodhisattva uses the methods of restraint to suppress all afflictions; because the afflictions are rendered powerless by such suppression, he is able to accumulate the roots of goodness that constitute the provisions for awakening.
By accumulating roots of goodness, one fulfills one's original vows and is able to reach bodhi.
Question:
Why does one not extinguish all afflictions through the path of annihilation?
Answer: The nature of a bodhisattva’s afflictions is not the nature of nirvāṇa;
it is not by burning away the afflictions that the seeds of bodhi are produced.
Just as the noble śrāvakas and others have nirvāṇa as their nature, because they attain the fruits of the śramaṇa by taking nirvāṇa as their object of focus;
the Buddhas do not have nirvāṇa as their nature, but rather afflictions as their nature, because the bodhicitta arises from them.

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas burn away all afflictions (*kleśa*) and do not produce the seed of the bodhicitta, because the seeds of the minds of the two vehicles are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, afflictions constitute the *tathāgatagarbha*; for it is through the afflictions of sentient beings that the bodhicitta is generated and the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*) is produced. Thus, one does not depart from afflictions.
Question:

If the seeds of the bodhicitta do not arise when the afflictions are burned away, why does the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas who have burned away their afflictions?
Answer: To bestow predictions upon those sentient beings, this prediction has its causes and conditions;
it is solely the Buddha’s skillful means that reach the further shore.

One does not know which sentient beings have been brought to maturity therein; the causes and conditions within that state are known only by the Buddha, for he has reached the further shore of subduing others and is thus not similar to other sentient beings.
And those who do not produce the seed of the bodhicitta do so because they have entered the state of the correct determination of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As it is said in a sutra:
"Like space and a lotus flower, / A steep precipice and a deep pit..."
The *dhātu* of one who is not a male, such as a *khañja*, is like a burnt seed;

just as seeds do not grow in the midst of empty space, so too within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) the Buddha-dharmas have never arisen and shall not arise, just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or in the wilderness.
In this way, when śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas enter the state of the correct determination of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-samyaktva-niyāma*), they do not give rise to the Buddha-dharmas.

Regarding "precipices": on the path to the city of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), there are two precipices, namely, the precipice of the śrāvaka stage and the precipice of the pratyekabuddha stage.
If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possessed all-encompassing wisdom, they would not be the two steep precipices for Bodhisattvas.
As for the deep pit: it is like a man who has skillfully practiced jumping; even if he falls into a deep pit, he remains there in safety and composure.
If one does not train well and falls into a deep pit, one dies within that pit.

In this way, because a bodhisattva practices the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in skillful association with it, although they practice the unconditioned, they do not fall into the midst of the unconditioned.
When śrāvakas and others cultivate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in association with what is unwholesome, they fall into the midst of the unconditioned.

As for the "realm" (*dhātu*), because śrāvakas are bound within the realm of the unconditioned, they are no longer able to act within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) does not arise therein.

One who is not a man is like a eunuch who no longer has any interest in the benefits of the five desires; likewise, a śrāvaka who possesses the unconditioned dharma has no further interest in the benefits of the Buddha-dharma.
As for *kacchā*, it is like a *kacchā* gem; although the gods and those of the world may skillfully polish that *kacchā* gem, they can never turn it into a *vaiḍūrya* jewel.

In this way, although a śrāvaka may possess the training in all the precepts, numerous merits, samādhis, and so forth, they will ultimately never be able to sit at the site of awakening and realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
It is also like a scorched seed: just as a scorched seed, though placed in the earth, watered, and warmed by the sun, can never sprout;
so too, once the seeds of affliction have been scorched by the śrāvakas, there is no possibility of rebirth within the three realms.
Based on such sūtras as these, one should know that once the śrāvakas have attained the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), they do not give rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
