The Fundamental Treatise by the Holy Nāgārjuna, with the Commentary by the Bhikṣu Īśvara,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of South India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
Question:
How should a bodhisattva who has attained power practice among sentient beings? Answer:
All treatises and crafts, as well as various activities involving clear arts and techniques.

For the sake of benefiting the world, these are produced and established. Among them are treatises on writing, seals, calculation, mineralogy, medicine, and the methods for subduing spirits, exorcising possession, and neutralizing poisons; treatises on villages, cities, gardens, groves, rivers, springs, ponds, and forests, as well as medicinal herbs and woods; treatises revealing the nature of gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, stones, white coral, and other precious gems; treatises recording and explaining the sun, moon, stars and planets, earthquakes, and the interpretation of dreams; and treatises on the characteristics of the various limbs and joints of the body. Such immeasurable treatises as these, which are able to provide benefit and happiness to the world, all perish and vanish when the kalpa undergoes dissolution; yet when the kalpa begins to evolve again, they are once more produced and established among human beings.

Furthermore, he causes to arise and establishes all various crafts such as those involving wood, iron, tiles, and copper; various esoteric arts capable of extinguishing afflictions such as possession by spirits, insanity, poisoning, cholera, and indigestion; and various activities such as carving, painting, embroidery, and weaving that bring benefit and happiness to the world.
Following those beings who are capable of being transformed, throughout the realms, destinies, and births,
they go to those places immediately according to their thought,

taking birth there by the power of their vows. These Mahāsattvas, in whichever world— whether among the destinies of devas and humans, or among births as brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and so forth— if there are beings capable of being transformed in those various places, they give rise to immeasurable thoughts for the sake of transforming those beings.

In accordance with the karmic retribution of the voices—whether long or short, broad or narrow—of those various classes of beings, one should make vows so as to enable sentient beings to undergo transformation; one should give rise to such karmic retribution of voices—long or short, broad or narrow—in order to cause those sentient beings to quickly undergo transformation.
Regarding various evil deeds, as well as toward sentient beings who are deceitful and illusory, one should don firm armor and mail; do not grow weary, nor should you be afraid.

Even if such evils as reviling, threatening, inciting fear, resentment, flogging, binding, imprisoning, and rebuking are heaped upon me, and even if I find that sentient beings are so immeasurably deceitful and illusory as to be incorrigible, for their sake I must not slacken my armor and mail. Furthermore, do not grow weary of saṃsāra, and do not be afraid of seeking bodhi.
Furthermore, one should give rise to this thought:
"I do not don this armor for the sake of sentient beings who are already free from flattery and deceit; I am donning this armor specifically for those very sentient beings."
"I shall initiate such diligence as to perform these deeds, so that those sentient beings may swiftly establish themselves in freedom from flattery and deceit.
In this way, one should firmly don the armor of self-vow.
Question:
You have already explained the practice of bodhisattvas who have attained power.
What is the practice of bodhisattvas who have not yet attained power?
Answer: Endowed with a supremely pure mind, without flattery or deceit,
one confesses all evil deeds and conceals all virtuous matters.
"Endowed with a supreme, pure intention" refers to the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), which is also an excellence of virtue.
"Intention" means the mind; thus, when that mind is fully possessed [of these qualities], it is called being "endowed with a supreme, pure intention."
"Neither flattery nor deception": flattery refers to a divergent mind;
a divergent mind means a lack of straightforwardness.
Furthermore, flattery is called a crooked mind, while deception refers to guile.
If the mind is neither crooked nor deceitful, that is to be without guile and without illusion.
Regarding "disclosing all evils": if one openly speaks of and discloses whatever evils one has committed, that is called disclosing all evils.
Regarding "concealing all good deeds": if one has performed virtuous actions and yet conceals them thoroughly, that is called "concealing all good deeds.
If a bodhisattva wishes to swiftly attain awakening, they should fulfill purity of mind, being without guile or deceit, confessing their misdeeds, and concealing their good deeds.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has said:
"Deceit is not bodhi; illusion is not bodhi.
Purify the karma of body and speech, and likewise purify the karma of mind."
One should cultivate the precepts of training so that they are not deficient.
Because these bodhisattvas wish to be endowed with the cultivation of mindfulness, they should first purify the actions of body, speech, and mind.

Among these, one should purify the three types of bodily misconduct—killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct—and should undertake their opposites, the three types of bodily wholesome conduct.

One should purify the four types of verbal misconduct—false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—and should undertake their opposites, the four types of virtuous verbal conduct.
One should purify the three types of unwholesome mental conduct—namely, greed, hatred, and wrong view—and should undertake their opposites, the three types of wholesome mental conduct.
One should also receive and follow the various *pārajika* and *mūlaka* training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Regarding those training rules, there should be no intentional violation despite knowing them.
If one’s precepts are deficient or leaking, the mind will not be settled during the cultivation of mindfulness.
Abiding in right mindfulness, he focuses his attention and reflects alone in solitude.
Using mindfulness as his own protection, his mind attains a state free from hindrances.

Having thus become perfectly pure in virtue, he abandons the five hindrances and goes to a secluded, clean, and remote place—where there is little noise, little clamor, and few mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, tigers, or thieves; where it is neither too cold nor too hot—and without laying down a bed, whether standing, walking, or sitting cross-legged, he fixes his mindfulness upon the tip of the nose or the region of the forehead, dwelling in concentration by properly gathering his mind upon a single object.
If the mind is restless toward sense objects, one should employ mindfulness as a gatekeeper.
Having thus established this protection, one remains far removed from the obstructing thieves of the mind; dwelling alone in a solitary place with an undistracted mind, one practices contemplation.
When conceptualization arises, one should discern what is wholesome and what is unwholesome;
one should abandon all that is unwholesome and extensively cultivate all that is wholesome.

If conceptualization arises during reflection, one should recognize that conceptualization at the very moment it arises; if it is unwholesome, one should immediately relinquish it so that it does not increase further, and if it is a wholesome factor, one should simply practice it repeatedly and extensively.
One should not allow the mind to be distracted, like a lamp in a room left unshielded from the wind.
If the mind that takes an object as its focus becomes scattered, one should recognize it through focused mindfulness and,
returning to that very object, cause it to abide wherever it moves.
When a bhikṣu practicing meditative concentration contemplates with his mind, he should focus his attention without distraction.

If the mind departs from its object, he should immediately become aware of it; even before it has wandered far from the object, he should withdraw the mind and cause it to abide securely within that object.

Just as a monkey tied with a rope is bound to a pillar and can only circle around that pillar but not go elsewhere, so too should one bind the monkey of the mind to the pillar of the object with the rope of mindfulness; it can only repeatedly circle around the pillar of the object and not go elsewhere.
One should not practice diligence with laxity or through wrong grasping;
because such [diligence] cannot sustain meditative concentration, one should therefore always cultivate it.
"Laxity" refers to being devoid of exertion and effort; "wrong grasping" refers to not grasping correctly, meaning that it is too intense.
If one wishes to achieve samādhi, one should not practice with laxity nor engage in wrongly conceived diligence.
Because laxity and wrongly conceived diligence cannot sustain samādhi, the practitioner of meditative concentration should always practice correctly.
If one ascends the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
acting solely for the sake of self-benefit, one does not relinquish firm diligence.

If one wishes to ascend the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, acting solely for the sake of self-interest and for one’s own nirvāṇa, one should still not relinquish firm diligence day and night, but exert oneself in practice with vigor.
How much more so for a great man, who both delivers himself and delivers others—how could he not arouse a diligence a thousand times greater than that?

For this bodhisattva must deliver all sentient beings across the river of saṃsāra and must also deliver himself; how then could he fail to arouse a diligence exceeding by hundreds of thousands of millions those of the followers of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles?
Just as one has crossed the river of saṃsāra oneself, so too should one cross it for others.

To practice at different times or follow separate paths, or to practice other ways at the same time—such is not how one should cultivate meditative concentration; rather, one should take a single object as one's focus.

Now, on this single day, one should not practice a separate concentration for half the time and follow a different path during the remainder; rather, one should skillfully take an object as the focus within a single concentration, allowing the mind to follow that one object without turning toward any other place.
Have no greed for the body, nor cherish even life;
though one may protect this body, it is ultimately subject to decay and ruin.
One should give rise to such a thought:
Within this body of mine, there is only thin skin, thick skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bones, marrow, and so forth, which will ultimately wither and dry up;
this life-span of mine shall likewise come to an end.
"That man possesses diligence, the power of a man, and the vigor of a man; I too shall surely attain these.
If I have not yet attained them, I must not slacken in my diligence."
Even if one protects this decaying body for a hundred years, it is inevitably subject to destruction.
One must never be greedily attached to gain, honor, or fame;
rather, as if one’s head or clothing were on fire, one should practice diligently to fulfill one's aspirations.

Now, when staying overnight in the wilderness, do not wander about out of greed for body or life; when gain, honor, or fame arise, you should not become attached to them. For the sake of accomplishing your own vows, you should practice with swift diligence, as if your head or clothing were on fire.
One must immediately give rise to the supreme benefit;
it cannot be left until tomorrow, for tomorrow is far too distant. By what means can one preserve a life that lasts but a moment?
When one practices with such urgency as if one’s head or clothing were on fire, one must not wait for tomorrow, as tomorrow is far away.
If there were any benefit for my body, I would certainly exert myself.
One should give rise to this thought:
"By what cause can I preserve my life from the moment the eyes are opened until they are closed?"
I shall attain victory this very day; tomorrow is too far off, so do not wait for tomorrow.
Abiding in right livelihood, even as one eats the flesh of a beloved son, one should feel neither attachment nor aversion toward what is consumed.

A bhikṣu who practices such meditative discipline, whether in a village or within a monastic dwelling, should, having obtained food through begging in accordance with the Dharma and free from reproach, neither give rise to greed or attachment nor feel aversion toward it. He should dwell securely in right mindfulness, eating as if consuming the flesh of his own beloved child, solely for the sake of maintaining the body so that it does not perish and his life may endure, thereby upholding and protecting his pure conduct.
It is as it was said of old:
when a husband and wife were traveling through a wilderness, they ate the flesh of their own child together.
For what purpose, then, does one leave the household life?
"Have I finished what was to be done? Now, do I intend to do it?
As stated in the *Daśadharma-sūtra*, one should reflect in this manner:
For what purpose have I gone forth into homelessness?
Is it out of fear for my livelihood,
or is it in search of the state of a śramaṇa?
If one seeks to become a śramaṇa, one should reflect thus:
"Regarding the task of a śramaṇa, have I already accomplished it, have I not yet accomplished it, or am I accomplishing it right now?"

For those who have not yet acted or are currently acting, one should apply oneself with diligence for the sake of accomplishing the causes and conditions; as for me, having left the class of householders, I am called "one of a different class."
One should frequently reflect:
"My livelihood depends upon others; I too must perform distinct observances.
Am I free from reproach regarding my own precepts?"
Do wise fellow practitioners of the pure life have no further cause for reproach regarding my precepts?

I have already separated myself from all those who are dear and beloved; I do not dwell together with them. I belong to karma; I am born of karma; I experience and enjoy karma; karma is my kin, and I act in accordance with karma.
Whatever karma I have performed, whether good or evil, I myself shall experience its results.
How shall I pass my days and nights?
Do I delight in emptiness and stillness?
"Do I possess the qualities of a superior person?
Am I able to attain the noble and transcendent knowledge and vision?
When fellow practitioners of the pure life question me at a later time, I shall speak without shame."
One should frequently reflect upon these ten dharmas; that is to say, a bhikṣu practicing in meditative concentration should frequently reflect upon them:
observing that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and that if there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, then all demonic activities should be recognized and abandoned.

The conditioned refers to that which arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions; because it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is devoid of "mine"; and because it is conditioned, it is impermanent.
If something is impermanent, it is suffering because it is oppressed by other factors.
If it is suffering, it is non-self because it does not function with autonomy.
One should contemplate conditioned phenomena in this way.

All demonic activities that should be recognized and abandoned—whether they arise from oneself or from others, acting as causes for a lack of aspiration, causes for distraction, causes for procrastination, or causes for obstruction regarding the sūtras associated with the bodhicitta and the six perfections—all such things should be clearly understood.
Having fully awakened to and abandoned all these works of Māra, do not allow them to act with impunity.
With respect to the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the bases of psychic power, right efforts, the path,
and the four foundations of mindfulness, exert yourself with diligence in their cultivation.
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these are the five faculties (pañcendriya).
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these are the five powers (pañcabala).
Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—these are the seven factors of enlightenment.
The concentration of desire, the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation—these are the four bases of psychic power.

To prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising; to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; to give rise to unarisen wholesome states; and to maintain wholesome states that have already arisen—generating desire, exerting effort, applying mindfulness, and setting one's will—these are the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Right view, right discrimination, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration: these constitute the Noble Eightfold Path.
The body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
For the sake of cultivating these thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, one arouses diligent effort.
The mind is the cause for the successive arising of all that is beneficial, pleasant, and virtuous, as well as for all evil, turbid, and unwholesome roots; therefore, one should examine it well.
If the mind is tamed, guarded, restrained, and bound, it becomes the cause for the successive arising of all manner of benefits, peace, happiness, and wholesome deeds.
If they are not subdued, not guarded, not cultivated, and not restrained, they serve as the root for all that is unbeneficial, evil, and turbid.

Having understood this, one should thoroughly examine them by way of their characteristics of arising, abiding, and changing; because they do not abide within, without, or between; because the past, future, and present do not coexist; because they come from nowhere and go nowhere; because they do not abide even for a moment, a *lava*, or a *muhūrta*; and because they are like a magical illusion. One should thus examine them for the sake of cultivation.
Within these wholesome qualities, what do I increase day by day?
And what do I diminish?
One should examine this most thoroughly.
If, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught, wholesome dharmas such as giving can give birth to bodhi, then what increase or what decrease occurs to those wholesome dharmas in me?
One should always observe with such focused diligence, rising again and again throughout each day.
Seeing others gain increase in offerings, honor, and fame, one must never harbor even the slightest stinginess or envy; these are all things that should not be done.

If one sees other fellow practitioners of purity—whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—at a time when their gains, honors, and reputation are increasing, one should not give rise to even the slightest stinginess or envy.
Furthermore, one should reflect and give rise to this thought:

"I too rejoice in obtaining the requisites for sentient beings—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal supplies for the sick; I too rejoice in receiving the respect of both householders and those who have gone forth; and I too rejoice in possessing the praiseworthy Dharma."
Do not envy various realms; act like one who is dull-witted, blind, mute, and deaf, yet occasionally let out a lion’s roar to frighten the deer that are the non-Buddhists.

When you see others increasing their gains, honors, and fame, you should feel no longing or envy for such sensory objects as form. Although you are not actually dull-witted, blind, mute, or deaf regarding pleasant and unpleasant forms, sounds, scents, and tastes, you should nevertheless conduct yourself as if you were so.
If you possess the power and ability, do not remain perpetually mute; you should dispel delusions and break the bonds with the True Dharma.
When the time comes, for the sake of terrifying the deer-like heretics and for the sake of upholding the True Teaching, you must again roar the lion’s roar.
I have already explained the cultivation of the mind.
Now I shall explain the characteristics of cultivation, namely:
welcoming and seeing off, and one should show reverence to those worthy of respect.
By assisting others in accordance with their various activities;

by welcoming and seeing off those worthy of respect; by offering garlands when listening to the Dharma; and by performing acts of reverence such as repairing caityas—through these deeds, one shall obtain the mark of wheels on the hands and feet, which is also a precursor to having a great retinue.
Rescuing those who are being killed, one naturally increases [merit] without diminishing it;
by skillfully cultivating the karma of clear wisdom, one trains oneself and teaches others.

Because one rescues those who are being killed and brings them to liberation, protecting their lives through the causes and conditions for non-killing, and because one has long practiced and remained close to such karmic deeds, one shall obtain the mark of long fingers, the mark of level and even heels, and the mark of an upright body; these are the preliminary signs of longevity.

Because one increases the wholesome dharmas received from oneself and does not allow them to diminish, one shall obtain the mark of high insteps like a conch shell and the mark of body hairs that point upward; these two are the prior signs of the non-diminution of the Dharma.

By skillfully cultivating the sciences, arts, and crafts, both through one's own study and by teaching others, one shall obtain the *iṇīya* mark; this is a preliminary sign of swift gathering [of disciples].
Firmly receiving all supreme and wholesome dharmas,
Practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), And bestowing robes and food and drink—

By firmly receiving all most excellent wholesome dharmas and habitually practicing them extensively, one shall obtain the mark of well-established feet; this is the precursor sign of being able to accomplish one's tasks.

By practicing the four means of attraction—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—and by constantly cultivating them, one will attain the mark of webbed hands and feet; this is also a preliminary sign of swift gathering [of beings].

By practicing the giving of exquisite food, drink, and clothing, and by constantly associating with such acts, one shall obtain the marks of soft hands and feet and the mark of the seven elevated parts of the body; these two are the prior signs of obtaining exquisite food, sweet flavors, clothing, and so forth.
Not refusing those who beg, harmonizing with all kinsmen and relatives so that the family remains undivided, and bestowing dwellings and wealth—

giving whatever one possesses immediately upon the arrival of a petitioner because one does not oppose them— one shall obtain the mark of well-rounded upper arms and thighs; this is the precursor sign of mastery and self-discipline.

By dwelling together with one's kinsmen and friends in harmony, ensuring that they do not become estranged, and by reconciling those who have become estranged, one shall obtain the mark of the secret male organ being concealed within the body; this is a precursor sign of having many children.

Because one gives away dwellings, wealth, and goods, as well as excellent beds, coverlets, clothing, halls, palaces, and so forth, one shall obtain the mark of a golden complexion and the mark of fine, smooth, and thin skin; these two are the prior signs for obtaining excellent beds, coverlets, clothing, halls, palaces, and the like.

Parents and close relatives should be established in their respective places; as for those who ought to be established in their proper positions, they are the unsurpassed lords of sovereignty. Upādhyāya (translated in the Sui language as "Near Recitation";

formerly translated as "Upa-shang," which is abbreviated and erroneous), Ācārya (translated in the Sui language as "Right Practice"; formerly translated as "A-sha-li," which is also erroneous), parents, brothers, and others who are objects of veneration—these should be established in their respective places because they are the unsurpassed lords of sovereignty. Consequently, one shall obtain the mark of a single hair per pore and the mark of a white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*); these two are the preliminary signs of equanimity.
Even if they are but servants, one should accept their skillful speech and treat them with the highest respect; for they dispense medicine that heals all ailments.
"Dispensing medicine that heals all ailments" refers to providing medicine, attending to the sick, nursing them, and supplying food and drink to those who are ill.

Because he is attended and nursed such that his illness can be cured, he shall obtain the mark of the level and full space between the shoulders and the mark of the supreme taste among all tastes; these two are the precursors of having little illness.

Foremost in the performance of prior wholesome karma, with words that are subtle, smooth, and exquisite, and speech that is well-composed and righteous, there is nothing lacking in what precedes and follows. Regarding "foremost in the performance of prior wholesome karma":

this refers to encouraging others and acting as their leader in the construction of gardens, groves, assembly halls, public wells, flower ponds, food, drink, and flower garlands; building bridges over difficult terrains; and constructing monasteries, pleasure parks, and the like. Because one’s own giving exceeds that of others, one shall obtain the two marks of a universal and perfectly rounded body (*nigrodha-parimaṇḍala*) and the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*). These two are the premonitory signs of a supreme lord.

Regarding "subtle, smooth, and exquisite speech": because of his practice of truthful, subtle, and smooth speech throughout the long night, he shall obtain the mark of a broad and long tongue and the mark of the Brahma-voice; these two are the preliminary signs for obtaining the fivefold and the fivefold qualities of the vocal organ and its perfect sound.

Regarding the ten qualities of the voice that are complete with fivefold aspects: first, it is intelligible; second, it is easy to understand; third, it is pleasant to hear; fourth, it is not disagreeable; fifth, it is profound; sixth, it is far-reaching; seventh, it is without reproach; eighth, it is pleasing to the ear; ninth, it is eloquent and correct; tenth, it is unadulterated. Because there are two sets of these fivefold qualities, there are ten.

One who is skilled in speaking with right intention, by virtue of having spoken truthful words and words of right intention throughout the long night, shall obtain the mark of a lion’s teeth; this is the precursor sign of loving speech.

Regarding "there is no one before or after whom he does not provide offerings": although others may have such distinctions of before and after, he provides offerings to all without exception because his deportment is in accordance with the Dharma and his conduct is impartial. Consequently, he shall obtain the mark of even teeth and the mark of fine, smooth teeth; these two are the premonitory signs of having a virtuous and pure retinue.
He does not cause dissension among the retinues of others; he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness and never with a mind of aversion, regarding them all as virtuous friends.

He maintains a heart that embraces, consoles, and gathers in all sentient beings, and because he observes them with eyes free from greed, hatred, and delusion, he shall attain the mark of blue eyes and the mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king. These two are the preliminary signs of observing with eyes of affection.
I have already explained the karma that gives rise to the thirty-two marks of a great man; there are other various practices of bodhisattvas which I shall now explain.
One should act exactly as one speaks; by acting in accordance with what one says, others will place their trust in you.
One ought to act precisely as one has spoken.
If one acts exactly as one speaks, others will develop faith and will surely accept whatever teachings are given.
One should protect the Dharma, observe those who are negligent,
and construct nets of gold and jewels to cover the caityas.

Within this Dharma, one should protect oneself; furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who turn their backs on the Dharma and are heedless, one should also employ skillful means to observe them and lead them toward the Dharma.
Furthermore, at the stūpas of the Tathāgata, one should cover them with various jeweled nets in order to bring the marks and signs of excellence to fulfillment.
Those who desire beautiful women should give them after adorning them,
while also explaining the virtues of the Buddha and bestowing garlands of variegated light.
If there are those who seek female attendants, he immediately adorns the female attendants and gives them as a gift.
These female attendants are all exceptionally beautiful; by giving them as a gift, he ensures that whatever objects of affection his own mind desires are all fully satisfied.

Furthermore, by means of immeasurable and diverse ways of teaching the Dharma that extols the Buddha’s virtues, one should deliver these discourses in assemblies with a voice that is loud, exquisite, and pleasing to the mind, in order to attain the purity of all vocal qualities.

Furthermore, he gives away various ornaments that radiate manifold lights to delight the eyes and minds of others, in order to attain the fulfillment of all the secondary physical marks (anuvyañjana).
One should fashion images of the Buddha, seated upright upon excellent lotuses,
and within the six dharmas, cultivate shared joy. By fashioning Buddha-images from gold,

silver, pearls, shells, stones, and so forth, and having them sit upon excellent lotuses, one does so for the sake of attaining birth by transformation and for the sake of attaining the body of a Buddha.

The six factors of shared joy are: toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, possessing loving physical, verbal, and mental actions; sharing possessions without making distinctions; being complete in ethical discipline; and being complete in right view.
Among these six kinds of dharmas conducive to joy, one should repeatedly practice and cultivate them in order to gain a following and not be defeated by those of other doctrines.
One should offer what can be offered and never fail to offer;
even for the sake of one's life, one should not slander the Dharma taught by the Buddha, nor those who teach it.
There is nothing that should not be offered; among those who ought to be venerated are one's preceptors, teachers, parents, brothers, and so forth.

There is nothing that should not be offered, and there is nothing that should not be revered. Even for the sake of sustaining one's life, one must never slander the Dharma or those who preach the Dharma of the Buddha.
One should neither slander nor treat with contempt [the teacher], for the sake of protecting one's own roots of goodness and providing assistance.
One should scatter gold and jewels before the teacher and at the teacher’s *caitya*;
if there is anyone who forgets what they have recited, one should grant them mindfulness so that it is not lost.
One should scatter gold and silver over the teacher, and one should also scatter mani-jewels and gold over the Teacher’s Jewel Stūpa.
Bodhisattvas possess a samādhi called "Facing the Buddhas of the Present."
Abiding in these samādhis, one practices them manifestly throughout successive lives in order to attain the power of hearing and retaining [the teachings].

If there are sentient beings who have forgotten the sūtras they recited—treatises that lead to worldly benefit and happiness—one provides them with reminders so that they do not lose their bodhicitta, and so that they may attain mindfulness and direct knowledge.
Once you have reflected upon what is to be done, do not act with haste nor follow others;
do not place your trust therein among the non-Buddhists, devas, nāgas, or spirits.

Regarding the actions performed through body, speech, and mind, if they have not been reflected upon beforehand, one should not act with agitation nor follow others; one should practice in this manner.
If it were otherwise, then the arising of feverish distress would also be a cause for regret.
One should not place faith in wandering mendicants, such as the Nirgranthas and other non-Buddhists, nor among gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth.
The mind should be like a vajra, capable of penetrating all phenomena;
the mind should also be like a mountain, unmoved by any circumstance.
One should settle the mind so that it is like a vajra, for it possesses the power of wisdom and capability.
Regarding all mundane and supramundane phenomena, one should penetrate them as they truly are according to their own nature.
In placing the mind amidst all affairs, it should also be like a mountain, unmoved by the eight worldly concerns.
One should delight in discourse that transcends the world; do not delight in relying on worldly speech.
One should personally receive all merits and should likewise cause others to receive them.

There may be certain discourses that are able to transcend the world—whether they correspond to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; whether they correspond to the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); whether they correspond to the stages of a bodhisattva (bodhisattva-bhūmi); or whether they correspond to the stages of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha—one should take delight in such [discourse].
There may be forms of speech that rely upon the world and increase worldly attachment, being associated with greed, hatred, and delusion;

one should not take delight in such things. However, regarding those various precepts, trainings, and other sublime virtues praised by the virtuous which are to be undertaken, one should embrace them all and should also cause others to embrace these virtues.
One should cultivate the five entrances to liberation, cultivate the ten perceptions of impurity, and likewise cultivate the eight awakenings of a great man (mahāpuruṣa) through analytical practice.

Among these, the entrances to liberation are: first, preaching the Dharma for others; second, preaching the Dharma for oneself; third, reciting the Dharma for oneself; fourth, awakening to and contemplating the Dharma in accordance with it; and fifth, grasping whatever signs of samādhi are appropriate.
These are the five bases of liberation, which should be recollected and cultivated.

As for the ten perceptions of impurity, they are: the perception of bloating, the perception of lividness, the perception of festering, the perception of oozing, the perception of being devoured, the perception of dismemberment, the perception of scattering, the perception of being smeared with blood, the perception of the flesh falling away, and the perception of bones; these are the ten perceptions of impurity.
When greed arises, one should practice mindfulness, for its original purpose is to sever desire and greed.

Regarding the eight thoughts of a great man (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*) that should also be cultivated through discernment: among these are the eight thoughts of a great man, namely, "fewness of desires is the Dharma; abundance of desires is not the Dharma"—this is the first thought.
Contentment is the Dharma; lack of contentment is not the Dharma—this is the second.
Seclusion is the Dharma; worldly bustle is not the Dharma—this is the third.
To arouse diligence is the Dharma; indolence is not the Dharma—this is the fourth.
To abide in mindfulness is the Dharma; loss of mindfulness is not the Dharma—this is the fifth.
That entering meditative concentration is the Dharma and not entering meditative concentration is not the Dharma is the sixth.
That wisdom is the Dharma and the absence of wisdom is not the Dharma is the seventh.
Not delighting in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma, while delighting in frivolous discourse regarding what is not the Dharma—this is the eighth.
These eight realizations of a Great Man should be realized;
the eight unwholesome aids, such as excessive desire and so forth, should be severed.
The divine ear and the divine eye, Supernormal power and knowledge of others' minds,
As well as dwelling in the recollection of past lives— One should cultivate these five purified superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Among them, the divine eye, the divine ear, the recollection of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, and supernormal power— these five kinds of superknowledge should be practiced.
*Bodhicaryāvatāra-prakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Requisites for Enlightenment), Fascicle Five; *Bodhicaryāvatāra-prakaraṇa*, Fascicle Six.
Original by the Noble Nāgārjuna; Commentary by the Bhikṣu Īśvara.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of South India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
Question:
How is it practiced?
Answer: The four bases of psychic power are the roots—desire, energy, mind, and investigation;
the four immeasurables that sustain them are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Having cultivated and frequently practiced these four immeasurables, one attains mastery of the mind.
Having attained mastery of the mind, one enters the first dhyāna, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth.

Having attained dhyāna, he attains lightness of body and mind; because he is fully endowed with this lightness of body and mind, he gives rise to and enters the path of spiritual powers. Because he is fully endowed with the path of giving rise to and entering the spiritual powers, he then produces the bases of supernormal power—namely, desire, energy, mind, and investigation.
Among these, desire is directed toward the Dharma; diligence is the accomplishment of the Dharma; the mind observes the Dharma; and reflection is skillfulness regarding the Dharma.

When that bodhisattva possesses faith-understanding or functional mastery in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), their mind is sovereign and acts according to their will. Because they are well-matured and because they abide in their own fundamental power, they move through all places in accordance with their course, like the wind pervading space.

In this regard, once a bodhisattva has attained the four immeasurables and the four dhyānas, whether through resolute belief or through actual practice, they produce the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Compared to the divine eyes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, or those of learners (*śaikṣa*) as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva’s eye alone possesses superior power; it is more pure, more radiant, more preeminent, and more extraordinary. Unimpeded, that eye can perceive all worldly forms—whether coarse or subtle, distant or near—exactly as desired.

Thus he hears the sounds of devas, humans, animals, and so forth; thus he recollects and knows his own past lives as being boundless and limitless; thus he knows the minds of others, including their association with greed and other afflictions, up to eighty-four thousand variations; and thus he attains immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Because they have attained the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), they cause all sentient beings who ought to be disciplined to be fully disciplined.
One should contemplate the four elements as venomous snakes, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as an empty village,
and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as executioners.

Throughout the long night, although these four elements—earth and the others—are protected, nurtured, and sustained through the causes and conditions of various articles of enjoyment, they quickly become agitated; for they are ungrateful for such care, unreliable, and unworthy of trust. Therefore, one should contemplate them as being like venomous snakes, because they have no master and are devoid of "I" and "mine."

The various sense bases, such as the eye, harbor a host of six thieves; because they cause oppression and affliction and are fearsome, one should contemplate them as being like an empty village. Since they cannot be shielded against by communal cooperation, the giving of goods, or by breaking, beating, or punishing them, they are like executioners.
Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, one should observe them thus every day:
Revere the Dharma and the teacher of the Dharma; abandon stinginess regarding the Dharma as well;
let the teacher not withhold secrets, and let the listener not be distracted.
In this regard, there are four kinds of dharmas that can give rise to great wisdom, which one should receive and uphold:
one should respect both the Dharma and the teacher of the Dharma;
one should also abandon stinginess regarding the Dharma, and according to what one has heard and what one has studied and recited, one should expound it for others.
If there are those who desire the Dharma, the teacher should not keep his hands folded in secrecy;
the listener should not be distracted, meaning they should have no other desires.
Free from pride and free from expectation, one should act solely with a heart of compassion.
With a mind of respect and reverence, one should preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that are the marks of great wisdom; these should be received and upheld.
This means being far removed from self-exaltation and disparaging others because one is free from arrogance;
abandoning gain, honor, and fame because one has no expectation for them;
and, out of pure compassion for sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, respectfully honoring them and preaching the Dharma for their sake.
By means of these four dharmas, a bodhisattva is fully endowed with great wisdom and should accept [the teachings].
Never being weary of hearing them, and having heard them, reciting and upholding them all;
not deceiving the venerable field of merit, and likewise causing the teacher to rejoice.

One should never tire of hearing much; having heard it, one upholds the Dharma; having upheld the Dharma, one practices in accordance with the Dharma. One does not deceive those who are venerable or the field of merit, and causes the teacher to rejoice in this Dharma.
This is the cause for not forgetting the bodhicitta.
One should not look toward other households with a mind seeking honor and sustenance,
nor should one study worldly treatises for the sake of engaging in debate.
One should not visit the homes of others for the sake of receiving offerings or honor, except for the purpose of establishing the bodhicitta.
Nor should one study worldly treatises and the like with the desire to engage in debate, except for the purpose of increasing one's learning.
Do not, out of anger, disparage the bodhisattvas;
nor should you give rise to slander regarding dharmas you have neither received nor heard. Why is this?
To protect the causes and conditions for the arising of wholesome dharmas,
one should sever pride and arrogance; one should abide in the four noble lineages,
neither disparaging others nor exalting oneself.
One who has severed pride should humble their mind toward all sentient beings like that of a dog and eliminate the conceit of "I.
They should also abide in the four noble lineages—moderation in food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites—because they possess contentment with those noble lineages.
One should not disparage others, nor should one be self-exalting.
Whether an offense is real or unreal, one must not expose the faults of others;
do not seek out the failings of others, but rather recognize your own mistakes.
If a fellow practitioner of the holy life commits an offense—whether it be true or untrue—one should not expose it.
One should not seek out the faults of others; rather, one should only be aware of one's own faults.
Regarding the Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas, one should not harbor doubts through discrimination;
though the Dharma is most difficult to believe, one should have faith within it.
One should not engage in discrimination regarding the Buddha, for the World-Honored One is fully endowed with unprecedented qualities (*āścarya-dharma*).
Furthermore, one should not harbor doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha-dharma, for it is a unique teaching (asādhāraṇa-dharma) among all sentient beings.
Moreover, because one possesses a deeply pure mind, one should place faith in this Buddha-dharma, which is most difficult to believe.
Even if one must die because of truthful speech, or even if one loses the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) or a king of the gods, one should speak only the truth.

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of truthful speech, should lose his possessions or even his life—even if he thereby forfeits the rank of a universal monarch or a king of the gods—he should still speak only the truth; how much more so should he refrain from speaking untruths in other circumstances?
Whether beaten, reviled, threatened, killed, or bound, one should never resent or blame others;
all these are my own faults, appearing now as the fruition of karma.
Whatever beating, reviling, threats, killing, binding, or imprisonment comes from others, it is all due to one's own sins and ought to be so; one should never harbor anger toward others.
"This is my own karma; having been committed in previous lives, I now receive a corresponding and undesirable fruit.
Those other sentient beings are entirely without fault; it is only the retribution for my own sinful karma that has manifested, and thus this must be so."
One should show the utmost respect and love, making offerings to one's parents and attending upon one's preceptors (upādhyāya); one should also revere one's teachers (ācārya).

Toward one's parents, one should show extreme love, respect, and provide offerings; one should regard them as deities, acting in accordance with their wishes to bring them joy, and remaining free from a mind of flattery or deception.

Furthermore, one should respectfully serve and attend upon one's preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya); regarding whatever Dharma they preach, there shall be nothing kept secret within, for it is all intended for external transformation.
To teach the most profound Dharma to those who believe in the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle— this is a bodhisattva’s error.
In this regard, there are four kinds of bodhisattva errors that should be abandoned.
To preach the most profound Dharma to sentient beings belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is an error for a Bodhisattva.
To preach the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to sentient beings who have faith in the profound Mahāyāna is likewise an error.
To preach the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to those sentient beings who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna is a mistake for a Bodhisattva.
When great beings come seeking the Dharma, to be negligent and fail to teach them,
while instead embracing the wicked and entrusting authority to those without faith, is a mistake for a Bodhisattva.

If a great being who is correctly established comes with a request, one should immediately explain the wholesome Dharma to them, yet instead, one acts with negligence toward the unwholesome Dharma of breaking precepts and even accepts such things;
this is an error of the bodhisattva.

To place one's trust in those who have not yet developed faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna, and who have not been brought to maturity through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), is a mistake for a bodhisattva.
These constitute the four kinds [of such mistakes].
One should distance oneself from the four types of errors described here,
for they keep one far from awakening; yet one should remember and understand the many virtues that have been explained, and likewise cultivate and draw near to them.

If, among those qualities such as the *ṛddhipāda*s and others taught in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one knows that they do not constitute obstacles to bodhi, then one should also cultivate and rely upon each of them.
Teaching with an impartial mind, establishing [beings] in equanimity,
and causing them to be correctly aligned— without distinction among all sentient beings—
these four paths of the bodhisattva should be practiced and cultivated.
What are the four? They are:

giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; preaching the Dharma with equanimity toward all sentient beings; skillfully establishing all sentient beings in equanimity; and causing all sentient beings to enter into correct correspondence.
All these are without distinction; they constitute the four kinds [of bodhisattvas].
They act for the sake of the Dharma and not for profit; they act for the sake of virtue and not for fame;
they desire to liberate sentient beings from suffering and do not desire their own personal happiness.
These four kinds of true bodhisattvas should be recognized.
What are the four? They are:

acting solely for the sake of the Dharma and not for material gain; acting solely for the sake of merit and not for reputation; desiring only to liberate sentient beings from suffering and not seeking personal peace and happiness.
Seeking the fruits of karma with intentional resolve, one performs meritorious deeds;
these arise for the sake of maturing sentient beings, having abandoned one's own affairs.

If one seeks to perform the three types of meritorious deeds with the intentional resolve for the fruits of karma, when these merits arise, they are solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings through enlightenment, and solely for the sake of maturing sentient beings through enlightenment; for the sake of benefiting others, one abandons one's own affairs.
These are the four kinds of true bodhisattvas who draw near to spiritual friends: namely, the Dharma-preacher, the Buddha,
those who encourage one to leave the household life, and those who beg for alms.
These four kinds of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) for bodhisattvas should be approached.
What are the four? They are:
first, the Dharma-preacher as a spiritual friend, for the purpose of assisting in the maintenance of the wisdom derived from hearing.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is a spiritual friend to bodhisattvas, for he assists them in upholding all Buddha-dharmas.
Those who encourage one to leave the household life are spiritual friends to bodhisattvas, for they assist them in upholding all roots of goodness.
Those who beg are the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends, for they assist in upholding the bodhicitta.
These four kinds of bodhisattva spiritual friends should be approached and relied upon.
Those who rely on worldly treatises, those who seek exclusively for worldly wealth,
and those who have faith in and understanding of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle as well as the Śrāvaka Vehicle—
these four types should be known as a bodhisattva’s bad friends.
What are the four? They are:
being a proponent of worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), because of cultivating and approaching various kinds of mixed eloquence;
and grasping at worldly wealth and possessions, because of not grasping the Dharma.
Because those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle have little benefit and perform few deeds,
and because those of the Śrāvaka vehicle act for their own self-interest—
these four types of evil associates are what a bodhisattva should recognize.
Furthermore, there are those who should be sought after, namely the four great treasuries.
As previously stated, the four kinds of "knowledge" (jñāna) are actually evil associates; having recognized them as such, one should distance oneself from them.
Furthermore, there are things that should be sought and attained, namely the four great treasuries.
When the Buddha appears, one hears of the various perfections;
having seen them at the abode of the Dharma Master, one’s mind is free from obstruction, and one delights in dwelling in secluded places.
These four kinds of great treasuries of the bodhisattvas should be attained.
What are the four? They are:
serving the supramundane Buddhas; hearing the six pāramitās; beholding the Dharma-preachers with an unobstructed mind; and dwelling joyfully in secluded places with heedfulness.
These are the four great treasuries of the Bodhisattvas, which one should attain.
Like earth, water, fire, wind, and space, they are entirely similar to them;
equal in all places, they benefit all sentient beings.

There are two causes and conditions by which one resembles a Bodhisattva in relation to earth, water, fire, wind, and space; these should be embraced, namely: because of equanimity and because of benefiting others.
Just as the five elements, such as earth and the others, as well as space, are equal in all places—whether there is mind or no mind—and possess no distinct characteristics;
they are constantly utilized by all sentient beings, yet remain without change and do not seek any recompense.
I am likewise; until the ultimate end at the site of enlightenment, I shall serve as a resource for all sentient beings, remaining without change and seeking no recompense.
One should properly contemplate the meaning and diligently give rise to dhāraṇīs;
do not create obstacles for those who listen to the Dharma.
"Meaning" refers to the meaning spoken by the Buddha; one should properly contemplate it whether in conversation with others or when dwelling alone; one should act in this manner.

Furthermore, one should abide in the purity of the precepts with a clear and pure mind, diligently cultivating fresh and stainless qualities, and listen to the *dhāraṇīs* such as the "Lord of Silver" and the "Lord of the Ocean.

Moreover, regarding those who listen to the Dharma, one must not create obstacles even for the slightest reason, in order to avoid the karmic retribution arising from calamities concerning the Dharma.
One should be able to subdue afflictions within oneself; Minor matters should be abandoned without remainder, And the eight kinds of slothful states Should all likewise be eliminated.

Regarding "one should be able to subdue afflictions within oneself": therein are nine kinds of afflictive matters. Namely, that [others] act, have acted, or will act to one's disadvantage—these constitute three types.

Regarding those who are dear to me, they have acted, are acting, and will act in ways that are unbeneficial; conversely, regarding those whom I dislike, they have acted, are acting, and will act in ways that are beneficial.
Those things already done, those being done now, and those yet to be done constitute another three types.
All of these constitute causes of affliction.
Among these nine kinds of causes of affliction, one should practice self-discipline.

Regarding the abandonment of minor factors without remainder, there are twenty such minor factors therein: namely, (1) lack of faith, (2) lack of shame, (3) guile and deceit, (4) restlessness, (5) distraction, (6) heedlessness, (7) harmfulness, (8) lack of dread, (9) laziness, (10) sorrow, (11) lethargy, (12) drowsiness, (13) resentment, (14) concealment, (15) envy, (16) stinginess, (17) arrogance, (18) anger, (19) regret, and (20) despondency.
These twenty kinds of minor matters are all to be abandoned without remainder. Regarding the eight kinds of slothful matters that should also be eliminated and severed:

among them are these eight types of slothful states. Namely: (1) "I wish to perform some task, so I shall lie down at ease and not exert diligence"; (2) "I have finished performing my task"; (3) "I am on the road"; (4) "I have finished walking the road"; (5) "My body is exhausted and cannot practice the work"; (6) "My body is heavy and cannot practice the work"; (7) "I have fallen ill"; (8) "My illness has cleared, but before long I shall lie down at ease and not exert diligence."
For these reasons, one should attain what ought to be attained, reach what ought to be reached, and realize what ought to be realized.
Regarding these eight types of indolence, one should exert diligence in order to eliminate and sever them.
Do not harbor improper greed; do not crave at random what is unsatisfactory.
Reconcile those who are separated, whether they be kin or strangers.
If you see beings endowed with abundant gains, fame, happiness, renown, and merit, do not harbor improper greed toward that abundance of fortune.
Because a greedy mind that acts improperly does not accord with one's true intent, it is therefore something one should not do.

Furthermore, among sentient beings who are mutually disputing and causing division, one should—without distinction between those who are kin and those who are not—cause them all to become harmonious, of one mind, and to love one another.
Having attained emptiness within emptiness, the wise do not rely on its practice.
If one were to attain emptiness, that would be an evil fault worse than the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Because emptiness uproots the great mass of ignorance, the wise do not rely on the attainment of emptiness in their conduct.
If one practices by relying on the attainment of emptiness, then even those with the fault of being difficult to cure—the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—can be cured.

This is because all modes of viewing are brought to liberation through emptiness. However, if one becomes attached to the view of emptiness itself, they cannot be cured, for there is nothing further that can bring about their liberation.
Sweeping and plastering, as well as various kinds of musical instruments, incense, garlands, and other articles of offering—these should be used to make offerings at a caitya.

At the sites of the Tathāgata’s caityas and images, one should perform offerings by sweeping and plastering the ground, and by using incense, garlands, burning incense, powdered incense, flower canopies, banners, and flags as ornaments for worship. This is done in order to attain the mastery of the fragrance of morality and physical beauty.

With conch shells, flutes, harps, waist-drums, large drums, thunder-drums, clapping hands, and various other musical instruments, they made offerings for the sake of attaining the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
They fashioned various circular lamps and offered them at the *caityas*,
as well as parasols, leather sandals, and vehicles such as horses and carriages.
Within a caitya, one should perform excellent offerings with various kinds of fragrant oils, butter lamps, garlands, and so forth, for the sake of attaining the Buddha-eye.

One should give gifts such as parasols, sandals, leather shoes, elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, for the sake of easily attaining the unsurpassed vehicle of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers.
One should exclusively take delight in the Dharma; one should delight in knowing that the attainment of faith in the Buddha is gained through this.
One should delight in serving the Saṃgha and likewise delight in hearing the True Dharma.
In this regard, a bodhisattva should always thus delight in the Dharma, and not delight in the pleasures of the five desires or worldly merit.
You should know that regarding the benefits obtained from faith in the Buddha, one must not merely believe in and delight in seeing his physical body (rūpakāya).
Within the Saṃgha, one should constantly and joyfully attend to them with all manner of requisites for comfort, rather than merely delighting in going to pay formal visits and inquiries.
One should always delight in hearing the Dharma without ever becoming weary or satisfied; do not merely take pleasure in hearing its words for a brief moment.
One should contemplate all phenomena as being unarisen in the past, non-abiding in the present, and non-arriving in the future.
Due to the power of the harmony of causes and conditions, and because they come from nowhere, they do not arise in the past;
due to their moment-by-moment disintegration and lack of abiding, they do not abide in the present;
and because they cease without remainder and go nowhere, they do not reach the future.
One should contemplate all phenomena in this way:
bestowing good things upon sentient beings without seeking any favorable recompense from them;
one should endure suffering alone and not seek to enjoy happiness for oneself exclusively.
A bodhisattva should benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings through virtuous deeds, yet should not personally desire such benefit and happiness for those beings.
Furthermore, when sentient beings possess immeasurable marks of suffering, I alone shall endure them on their behalf.
I possess articles of enjoyment which I share with all sentient beings for their pleasure.
Though I am fully endowed with great merit and rewards, my mind neither exults nor rejoices;
though I may be as poor as a hungry ghost, I neither sink into despondency nor feel sorrow.
Although one may dwell among the gods who possess great and complete merit and reward, the mind should neither feel joy nor elation.

Although one may be a hungry ghost, destitute, ruined, and oppressed by the most difficult conditions for survival, one should not give rise to a sense of inferiority, nor should one be sorrowful; how much less so when it concerns the poverty and ruin of the human realm?
If there are those who have already studied, one should respect them most deeply;
one should cause those who have not yet studied to enter into study, and should never give rise to contempt.
If there are sentient beings who have already studied, one should treat them with the utmost respect.
If there are those who have not yet studied, one should cause them to enter into study and must not treat them with contempt.
One should revere those who possess the precepts and lead those who have broken them back into the precepts;
one should draw near to those who possess wisdom and establish the foolish in wisdom.

One who is fully endowed with the precepts should be greeted with inquiries after their well-being, saluted with palms joined, and honored with respect; one should also explain to them the merit of observing the precepts.
As for those who have broken the precepts, one should cause them to enter into the precepts and should also explain to them the transgression of breaking the precepts.
One who is endowed with wisdom should be approached and associated with, and one should also manifest the virtues of wisdom to them.
One should cause the foolish to abide in wisdom, and should also expound upon the faults of ignorance to them.
The sufferings of saṃsāra are manifold: birth, old age, death, and the evil realms.
One should not fear such terrors; rather, one should subdue the evil wisdom of Māra.

Within the cycle of saṃsāra, the Bodhisattva undergoes various transmigrations, including birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, as well as the evil realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras. He should not be afraid of these, but should instead solely subjugate the evil Māra and his evil wisdom.
All the Buddha-fields, having gathered together all merits, are for the sake of attaining them all; thus one generates vows and exerts diligence.

Whether it be the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions—whether those Buddha-lands are fully endowed or adorned, whether heard from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas or seen by oneself—all of these gather together supreme merits, causing them all to enter into one’s own Buddha-land.
One should make such vows; as one vows, so shall it be accomplished. One should likewise practice with diligent effort.
Always, amidst all phenomena, one should practice relinquishment without grasping;
this is for the sake of all sentient beings, to take up and bear their burden.
Because of grasping there is suffering; because of non-grasping there is happiness.
Having formed this thought, one should always relinquish all phenomena without grasping.

Although one relinquishes them without grasping, if previously—for the sake of attaining bodhi—one made a vow to take up the burden of sentient beings, thinking: "Those who have not been delivered, I shall deliver; those who have not been liberated, I shall liberate; those who have not attained peace, I shall bring to peace."
This burden should be taken up for the sake of all sentient beings.
Contemplate all phenomena correctly as being without self and without what belongs to a self;
yet do not abandon great compassion and great loving-kindness.
It is taught that all phenomena are non-existent, for they are like dreams and illusions.
All phenomena are selfless; those who possess no sense of "mine" contemplate the signless.
Thus, when one contemplates these signs through the dharma of the supreme ultimate meaning, one nevertheless does not abandon great compassion and great loving-kindness toward sentient beings.
Thus, one should again and again weigh this matter and exclaim in wonder: "How marvelous!
Those sentient beings, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and clinging to 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' do not perceive or understand this most supreme path of the Dharma."
"When shall I cause those sentient beings to awaken to this most supreme path of the Dharma of ultimate meaning?
This is what it means to not abandon great compassion and great loving-kindness toward sentient beings.
That which surpasses all other offerings by making offerings to the Buddha,
the World-Honored One— what is it?
It is what is known as the offering of the Dharma.

If there are those who offer various articles of worship to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—namely, offering flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, lamps, and wheels; or offering parasols, banners, and flags; or offering music and the like; or making offerings through the giving of medicines and delicious food and drink.
If one wishes to surpass all those other offerings, one should make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, what is this?
The answer is: it is so-called "Dharma-offering."
What further characteristics does that offering of Dharma possess?
If one upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, attains dhāraṇīs,
and enters the profound depths of the source of the Dharma— this is the offering of Dharma.

Among these, those that correspond to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka—such as the sūtras and other teachings spoken by the Tathāgata—are characterized by profound clarity, turn away from all worldly things, are difficult to fathom and difficult to perceive in their subtle details, are unattached and definitive in meaning, and are sealed with the seal of the King of Sūtras, the dhāraṇī.

The causes for non-retrogression arise from the six perfections; they skillfully encompass that which is to be grasped and accord with entry into the factors conducive to awakening, harmonizing with the nature of perfect enlightenment.
They enter into great compassion while preaching great loving-kindness; they remain free from the views of Māras and skillfully explain dependent origination.
They enter into the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a life-principle, the absence of a nourishing soul, and the absence of a person, and they are in accord with emptiness.
In conjunction with the signless, the wishless, and the unconditioned, he sat at the site of enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma,
praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas; he crossed over the mire of householders, gathered in all the noble ones,
expounded the practices of the bodhisattvas, and entered into the dharma, its meaning, its phrasing, and its eloquence.
The eloquence of this teaching resounds with the thunderous voice of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth;

it strikes terror into the various externalist treatises and their attachments to views and acquisitions. Praised by all Buddhas, it serves as the antidote to cyclic existence and reveals the bliss of nirvāṇa.
To preach, uphold, observe, and assimilate such sutras as these is called the offering of Dharma.
Furthermore, the offering of Dharma consists in attaining non-retrogression by practicing in accordance with the *dhāraṇī*.

To enter to the very depths of the profound dharmas associated with emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action, remaining unmoved and free from doubt—this is called the supreme offering of Dharma within the ultimate sense.
One should rely upon the meaning, not merely on the variety of flavors;
within the profound path of the Dharma, enter skillfully and do not be negligent.

Furthermore, as for the offering of the Dharma: if one contemplates the Dharma and practices the Dharma within the Dharma, conforming to dependent origination and remaining free from all views of extreme grasping, one attains the patience of non-arising and non-origination, enters into non-self, and within the sphere of causes and conditions remains without contradiction, strife, or contention, being free from "I" and "mine."
One should rely on the meaning, not on the fond pursuit of various ornamental words and phrases.
One should rely on wisdom, not on consciousness.
One should rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, not cling to the conventional expressions of sūtras of provisional meaning.
One should act in accordance with the Dharma and not adopt the views of others.

One should follow the practice of the Dharma as it truly is and enter the state of non-abiding; one should skillfully contemplate that ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are all utterly extinguished.
Having thus contemplated dependent origination, one brings forth the inexhaustible; out of compassion for sentient beings, one does not cling to various views and does not practice negligence.
If one always acts in this manner, it is called the unsurpassed offering of the Dharma.
In this way, through these provisions, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
those who have gone forth and those who remain at home shall attain the fulfillment of perfect awakening.

As previously described regarding these provisions, throughout eons as vast in measure as the sands of the Ganges, the bodhisattvas of both the monastic and lay communities will, over a long period, fulfill their aspirations and achieve perfect awakening.
I have appended these verses on the provisions for enlightenment;
they contain the meaning of the provisions without omission, just as they appear in those original verses.
Now, having selected those verses, there may be some increase or decrease in their meaning.
Those who are wise and virtuous should endure it, for they well understand the meaning of these verses and so forth.
Having explained these verses on the provisions, may whatever merit and goodness I have performed lead all wandering beings to attain Perfect Enlightenment.
The *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra* composed by the noble Nāgārjuna is hereby concluded; I, the bhikṣu Svatantra, have finished my commentary.
